articles.headline: Six-Neuron Networks Give Gaussian Splats High-Frequency Surface Detail
articles.lede: *3D Gaussian Splatting* has transformed neural scene reconstruction since its 2023 debut, representing environments as clouds of translucent ellipsoids that render in real time — but it handles fine surface texture poorly, forcing the system to multiply primitives wherever a checkerboard or fabric pattern appears. A CVPR 2026 paper by Haato Watanabe and Nobuyuki Umetani proposes a fix: attach a compact learned function to each Gaussian so it can express spatially varying color rather than a single shade. The result yields sharper reconstructions with fewer components.

articles.headline: Haplogroup X and the Mystery of the Missing Asian Trail
articles.lede: Of the five major mitochondrial DNA lineages found among Indigenous Americans, four trace cleanly back through Siberia and East Asia — the textbook Beringia route. The fifth, **Haplogroup X**, has no detectable footprint in northeast Asia. Its closest surviving relatives live thousands of miles away, in the Near East and Mediterranean.
articles.tweet_text: A DNA lineage in ancient North America has no trail through Siberia or East Asia. Its closest relatives are in the Near East and Mediterranean. If it didn’t come through Siberia, how did it get here? Haplogroup X: the genetic breadcrumb still rewriting the map.

articles.headline: Recurrent Feedback Closes the Gap in Instant 3-D Scene Reconstruction
articles.lede: The dominant paradigm for fast 3-D scene reconstruction has until now committed to a single forward pass: one neural-network prediction, no self-correction. ReSplat, from ETH Zurich and the University of Tübingen, breaks that pattern with a recurrent feedback loop that uses its own rendering errors to refine a scene in successive iterations — without computing gradients. The result is quality approaching slow per-scene optimisation at a fraction of the computational cost.

articles.headline: JSON as a Director's Brief: Prompting AI Video With Cinematic Precision
articles.lede: A thread by @techhalla closes with a worked example of a deceptively simple technique: a JSON object whose keys — *scene_description*, *visual_style*, *camera_movement*, *color_palette*, *dialog*, *subtitles* — translate cinematic vocabulary into a machine-readable prompt. The target platform, though unnamed, is almost certainly Google Veo 3, the only leading text-to-video tool with native synchronized speech and audio; the *dialog* and *subtitles* fields map precisely to that capability. The technique points toward a new creative literacy that sits at the intersection of film direction and software engineering.

articles.headline: Anthropic's $44 Billion Sprint: Parsing the Numbers Behind the Hype
articles.lede: Anthropic's annualized revenue has vaulted from nine billion dollars at the close of 2025 to a reported forty-four billion by early May 2026, a trajectory so steep it strains the vocabulary of normal corporate finance. A back-of-envelope profit-and-loss model making the rounds on X puts the company at roughly a billion dollars of EBITDA — but the arithmetic rests on assumptions that deserve scrutiny before anyone mistakes napkin math for audited accounts.
articles.tweet_text: Perhaps even more notable than Anthropic's $44B ARR figure is the reported 70% gross margins on inference. If you do some back of the napkin math and assume: - 75% of total rev. comes from AWS, GCP marketplaces for which Anthropic pays 25% rev. share ($8.25B total rev. share costs) - 2.5GW of total compute at $12B per GW ($30B total), with $13.2B on inference (to back into 70% gross margins) and $16.8B on training - 5,000 FTEs at $0.75MM in annual compensation per head ($3.75B total) - $1B of other OpEx (e.g. marketing, office rent, finance, legal etc.) ... Then total run-rate COGS + OpEx is $43B, implying $1B of EBITDA.

articles.headline: GaussianGPT Treats 3D Scene Generation Like a Language Problem
articles.lede: A team at the Technical University of Munich has built a model that generates complete 3D scenes by predicting one discrete spatial token at a time — the same next-token prediction paradigm that powers large language models, applied coherently to full-room scenes built from 3D Gaussian primitives. Where diffusion models refine a whole scene in parallel by gradually denoising a random field, GaussianGPT builds rooms incrementally, laying down voxels of compressed 3D data in sequence, which means a partial scene can serve as a prompt for completion or extension. The result is a single pipeline that handles unconditional generation, scene completion, and large-scale outpainting without architectural changes between tasks.
articles.tweet_text: GaussianGPT: autoregressive 3D Gaussian scene generation. We introduce a GPT-style model that directly generates 3D Gaussian scenes, token by token, in a series of small, discrete decision steps. Generation, completion, and large-scale outpainting in a single pipeline. Unlike diffusion-based approaches, GaussianGPT explicitly models the scene distribution at every step, allowing for quite flexible scene synthesis. https://nicolasvonluetzow.github.io/GaussianGPT/ https://youtu.be/zVnMHkFzHDg Great work by @nicolasvluetzow , @barbara_roessle , @katha_schmid

articles.headline: A Midjourney Engineer Ends the Web's 30-Year Text Layout Bottleneck
articles.lede: Every time a browser needs to know how tall a block of text is, it freezes, recalculates the position of every element on the page, and then answers. That single architectural constraint has quietly limited web design for three decades. Pretext, a 15-kilobyte JavaScript library released on March 27, 2026 by Cheng Lou, a senior engineer at Midjourney, bypasses it entirely — measuring text through the browser's Canvas engine instead of its layout tree.
articles.tweet_text: Every website you’ve ever used is broken in a way you never noticed and it’s been this way for 30 years... A Midjourney engineer finally just fixed it. It’s called Pretext: A tiny library that lets websites lay out text the way magazines and newspapers do, with text flowing around images, wrapping into columns, and fitting perfectly into any shape, all at 120fps. This has been basically impossible on the web for 30 years. Every website you’ve ever used relies on the same clunky system from the 90s to figure out where text goes on screen. Pretext bypasses it entirely. 500x faster. The demos look like they shouldn’t be possible in a browser. Go look.

articles.headline: A Painted Census of God's Warning Signs, Rediscovered After Centuries
articles.lede: The *Augsburger Wunderzeichenbuch* — the **Augsburg Book of Miracles** — is a lavishly illuminated manuscript of 169 pages assembled in Augsburg, Germany, around 1545–1552: a painted compendium of every extraordinary thing God had apparently sent to warn or instruct humanity. One of the most visually arresting documents of the Reformation era, the book spent roughly four and a half centuries lost to scholarship before resurfacing at a European auction in 2008. A Taschen facsimile edition, published in 2013, returned it to wide attention.

articles.headline: How Put-Option Mechanics Can Force a Market Bounce at Expiration
articles.lede: Options markets and equity markets are not separate arenas — they are the same game played on two boards simultaneously. When fear drives a surge of put-option buying, the dealers who absorb that demand are mechanically obligated to short the underlying shares. As expiration approaches and those obligations unwind, the resulting buying pressure can be structurally significant regardless of whatever fundamentals dominate the headlines.
articles.tweet_text: Layman's guide (no greeks) to understand why the stock market does what it does and seemingly doesn't make sense. 1. When you buy puts, the dealer that sold you those puts also just shorted actual shares to stay neutral, so they don't take a loss if the market tanks. 2. Those shorted shares need to be purchased back by that dealer prior to your option expiration date. 3. When skew gets lopsided to one side, you will see big moves going the other way. 4. When fear goes up, positions skew heavily to puts. This includes retail betting one-way for a market crash and large institutions who hedge their portfolios. 5. If 3-5 weeks ago, a lot of people bought April puts, A LOT of shares need bought back by April OPEX. We are here now. 6. The only way to keep going down at this stage is: A) for a fear event bigger than the previous one to cause new aggressive put buying or B) April OPEX dealer buybacks complete to level their books.

articles.headline: Splitting Robot Physics from Browser Rendering via WebSocket
articles.lede: A developer has built a proof-of-concept that runs **MuJoCo** physics simulation on a server while the browser handles only rendering, with a WebSocket stream carrying robot state between them. The demo features a Unitree G1 humanoid robot — a 29-degree-of-freedom biped — walking in synchronized views across both environments. The architecture is a deliberate inversion of the now-common approach of compiling physics engines to WebAssembly for fully in-browser execution.

Streaming robot state, rendering in Three.js, physics running server-side. Benefits: - Swap physics engines without touching renderer - No browser memory ceiling - Precise MuJoCo physics + beautiful Three.js visuals PoC done. Unitree G1 walking demo synced across both views. Working toward a clean streaming protocol. #robotics #mujoco #threejs

articles.headline: Skan Bodywork and the Body's Unsettled Emotional Record
articles.lede: When @seanta___ asked 'what was it?!' and @zencephalon replied with three words — Skan Reichian Bodywork — the exchange pointed to an obscure but earnestly theorized tradition of body-oriented psychotherapy with roots in pre-war Vienna and its contemporary practice concentrated in Hamburg. SKAN is a form of *body psychotherapy* that proceeds from a premise first articulated by Wilhelm Reich: that psychological defenses against trauma become encoded not only as mental habits but as chronic patterns of muscular tension — and can, with the right intervention, be released through the body directly. The name comes from the Lakota word *skan*, meaning 'that which moves,' chosen in 1982 to describe the felt sense of unobstructed energetic flow that the practice aims to restore.

articles.headline: OpenAI's Symphony Turns a Project Board into a Coding Factory
articles.lede: A specification from OpenAI called Symphony instructs a long-running daemon to watch a Linear project board, claim eligible issues, and dispatch each to an autonomous Codex agent that will — without human prompting — write code, open pull requests, and mark the ticket done. Released in spring 2026 and quickly accumulating 18,000 GitHub stars, it is less a product than a blueprint: a language-agnostic spec with a reference implementation in Elixir, designed to be copied and reimplemented. Its governing idea is that the right interface for managing AI coding agents is not a chat window but a project board.

articles.headline: An ANU Thesis Argues Consciousness Is the Optimal Learning Strategy
articles.lede: Michael Timothy Bennett, a doctoral candidate at the Australian National University, has published a thesis arguing that consciousness is not an evolutionary accident but the mathematically optimal solution to the problem of learning in an uncertain world. The 2025 work, *How to Build Conscious Machines*, draws on algorithmic information theory, philosophy of biology, and cognitive science to propose that *valence* — the primitive attraction or repulsion present even in single-celled life — scales up into the full machinery of human self-awareness. The argument, if it holds, would make the *philosophical zombie* computationally impossible and place current large language models categorically outside the bounds of consciousness.

articles.headline: What Really Protects Your Portfolio When Inflation Spirals
articles.lede: A 2021 paper by Campbell Harvey and the Man Group research team sifted 95 years of market data across the United States, Britain, and Japan to identify which assets hold their real value when inflation spirals above 5%. Their answer unsettles almost every standard portfolio construction of the past three decades: the workhorse 60/40 allocation turns from a reliable compounder into a reliable loser, and the most dependable protection comes from an active strategy most institutional investors barely allocate to.
articles.tweet_text: This paper is a banger. Worth revisiting.

articles.headline: Citrini's Three-Year AI Trade: 400% Return, One Pivotal Short
articles.lede: CitriniResearch's Dynamic AI portfolio crossed +400% total return in May 2026, roughly three years after its May 2023 inception, against approximately 254% for the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, the sector's standard benchmark. The portfolio's 46 holdings rotated systematically through AI infrastructure sub-themes — GPUs, optical networking, advanced packaging, power, and chip testing — as each layer hit its valuation peak. Its single largest contributor was not a long position but a short on that benchmark, placed the Friday before DeepSeek's January 2025 market shock.
articles.tweet_text: For almost 3 years now, since CitriniResearch’s first AI Infrastructure article in May 2023, we’ve published our Dynamic AI portfolio. It’s our longest running actively managed portfolio and just crossed +400% since inception. We have attempted to stay ahead of rotations within AI - everything from GPUs to optics to memory to power and more. Through every drawdown and rip of the majority of this cycle, our AI allocation has been transparently open for our subscribers. It’s one thing to write research, it’s another thing entirely to publish a collection of positions based on that research. At this point, we’ve written about 20 articles related to AI and it’s sub-themes - each one has has trades, some of which I certainly wish I’d held longer, some I wish I hadn’t put on and some I’m quite proud of. Funnily enough, the biggest single winner by contribution rate remains when we went short with 50% of the portfolio on SMH leading into the “DeepSeek” moment and covered in April. Another amusing thing, I’ve been covering the AI infrastructure trade for more than a thousand days now and I don’t think a single one of them has gone by without someone calling it a bubble. 3 years is a long time to trade a single theme, but every time that I think I’ve seen all this trend has to offer, it surprises me with something new. Curious what the next thing will be, and hopeful we’ll be ahead of it.

articles.headline: Higgsfield Steal Lets Anyone Clone a Creator's Visual Identity
articles.lede: A new feature from generative AI company Higgsfield promises to extract the visual character and style of any image found online and reproduce it on demand. The capability, branded as "Steal," runs on the company's *Soul ID* system — technology designed to lock in a subject's appearance across generated outputs. Its promoters frame it as democratisation; its critics will frame it as something closer to the literal word in its name.

articles.headline: The Candle That Saw Everything Coming — After the Fact
articles.lede: A trading account with 92,000 followers claims its proprietary ”Pink Smart Candle” predicted an 8.3% single-day drop in Avis Budget Group before it happened. The actual story of Avis in early 2026 — a historic short squeeze, a violent unwind, and a straightforward earnings miss — leaves little room for mysticism.
articles.tweet_text: CAR — The PINK candle told the story before it happened. Not after. Not during. Before. Your only regret? Not having a system this sound and this simple.

articles.headline: Carl Jung's Case for Walking Straight Into Your Fear
articles.lede: A spare tweet by @hamptonism points readers toward one of Carl Jung's more counterintuitive prescriptions: that fear, far from being an obstacle to sidestep, is the precise terrain a person must enter. The Swiss psychiatrist, who died in 1961, built a framework for the psyche in which avoided fear does not weaken — it compounds.
articles.tweet_text: Do yourself a favour, Look up what Carl Jung says about overcoming fear.

articles.headline: China's Factory Prices Have Deflated for Forty Straight Months
articles.lede: For more than three years, Chinese factory-gate prices have fallen without interruption — a streak that quietly compressed inflation worldwide even as Western central banks claimed victory over the post-pandemic price surge. The chart Danny Dayan shared captures the full arc: a brief positive plateau in 2022 that turned negative in October of that year and never recovered.
articles.tweet_text: Uh oh, the last domino has fallen

articles.headline: The Learning Science Schools Have Ignored for a Century
articles.lede: The gap between what scientists know about learning and what classrooms actually do is one of education's persistent embarrassments. A handful of techniques — backed by more than a century of replicated research — reliably outperform the methods most schools still use. Educator and adaptive-learning engineer Justin Skycak argues in this thread that the failure of adoption is structural, not informational: every incentive in the system rewards the wrong experiment.
articles.tweet_text: TLDR: There are numerous cognitive learning strategies that 1) can be used to massively improve learning, 2) have been reproduced so many times they might as well be laws of physics, and 3) connect all the way down to the mechanics of what's going on in the brain.

articles.headline: An AI Skill That Clones Any Website in One Prompt
articles.lede: A pseudonymous developer has published an open-source Claude Code skill that reconstructs any website — fonts, colors, layout, and animations intact — from a single slash command. The tool harnesses Claude Code's built-in Chrome browser extension to pull live assets directly from a running browser session, bypassing the guesswork of screenshot-based cloning. Within six weeks, the GitHub repository had accumulated more than 14,000 stars.
articles.tweet_text: Someone just built a Claude Code skill that clones any website perfectly in one prompt. It uses the built-in Chrome MCP to go straight to the source. It pulls the exact fonts, colors, and layout directly from the browser. 100% Open Source.

articles.headline: L-Tyrosine Is No Adderall — but That May Be the Point
articles.lede: A two-post exchange on X captures a familiar tension in nootropics culture: the desire for pharmaceutical-grade focus without the prescription. When @kodjima33 described a first Adderall experience as “coffee but 5x” and worried it might blunt creativity over time, @beffjezos offered a one-word redirect: *L-Tyrosine*. The suggestion is plausible — but the gap between the supplement’s marketing and its mechanism is larger than the recommendation implies.
articles.tweet_text: Try L-Tyrosine instead

articles.headline: A Plug-In That Teaches Claude Code Your Visual Language
articles.lede: Claude Code can refactor a database schema or wire up an API endpoint with few complaints, but ask it to design a user interface and the results tend toward the generic — purple gradients, boilerplate card layouts, the same dozen icons. AIDesigner is a newly released tool that tries to close that gap by embedding a purpose-built design engine inside Claude Code via Anthropic's Model Context Protocol. The trick is giving the AI a structured picture of the project's own visual conventions before a single component is drawn.
articles.tweet_text: someone just dropped a way to get insanely clean UI out of claude code the problem till now: - no context of your codebase - constant switching between tools - UI that doesn’t actually fit your project this fixes that, now claude can: - design inside your workflow - understand your system - generate UI that actually fits try it here - https://aidesigner.ai/docs/claude-code-mcp…

articles.headline: How Sound Frequencies Sculpt Living Patterns in Soap Film
articles.lede: A soap bubble, it turns out, is a remarkably sensitive membrane. Play a tone near one and it responds with elaborate geometry — rippling, folding, and freezing into forms that shift with every change in frequency. The practice of making those patterns visible is called **cymatics**, and its soap-film variant is among the most arresting demonstrations in all of experimental physics.
articles.tweet_text: Bubble cymatics never fail to mesmerize,shapes bending, light dancing, and distortion frozen in motion. Sound sculpting the surface into pure visual poetry. 299 people appreciated it will you be the next view? Link posted in comments as always

articles.lede: The saved post from @0ccultbot (June 6, 2025) could not be reconstructed from the available data. The bookmark record contains only engagement metadata — 9 replies, 31 reposts, 145 likes, 8.4K views — but no tweet body, image description, or linked content. All three research sources returned JavaScript-disabled errors from X.com and yielded no readable text.

Tripo AI is a platform that takes a single image and runs it through a full pipeline: mesh generation, retopology, texturing, rigging, and pre-built animations. The demo shown here suggests the whole chain now fits inside one browser-based tool.

articles.headline: The Chip the West Missed: MediaTek's Quiet Ascent from Budget Silicon to AI Infrastructure
articles.lede: For years, North American analysts filed MediaTek under "cheap Android chips" and looked away. As the Taiwanese fabless giant prepares to deliver two billion dollars of Google TPU silicon and eyes a quarter of the AI ASIC server market by 2028, that dismissal is looking expensive.
articles.tweet_text: Let’s admit what needs to be admitted. I was guilty of this as well, but North America-based analysts, across both the sell side and the buy side, have significantly underestimated MediaTek.

articles.headline: Google Brings No-Code Agent Orchestration to the Enterprise
articles.lede: At Cloud Next on April 22, 2026, Google unveiled the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, with **Agent Designer** as its centerpiece — a drag-and-drop canvas that lets business users wire together AI agents without writing a line of code. The pitch is familiar from the robotic-process-automation wave of the 2010s, but the underlying substrate has changed considerably.
articles.tweet_text: Build powerful workflows (no code required). With Agent Designer in Gemini Enterprise, you can orchestrate complex, specialized automations using a simple drag-and-drop interface.

articles.lede: “Most developers use Claude Code like a chatbot that happens to live in the terminal” — the opening line of the article this post links to, and an accurate description of a common failure mode. Anthropic’s coding tool ships with over sixty built-in commands, a persistent memory system, and a programmable automation layer; most of that surface goes undiscovered until something goes obviously wrong. A tweet dramatizes the gap: three months of declining output quality, resolved instantly by `/clear`, followed by the rueful discovery that commands exist at all.

articles.headline: Style Dropper Makes Aesthetic Transfer a Single Click
articles.lede: The hardest thing to transfer in design has never been a color or a typeface but the gestalt — the inarticulate sense of how a visual composition coheres as a whole. Variant, a San Francisco startup from Y Combinator’s Fall 2024 cohort, has built a tool called Style Dropper that claims to sample that holistic quality from any image and apply it to a generated interface in a single click. The reaction from designers who have seen the demo has been visceral.

articles.headline: America's Last Electrical-Steel Maker and the Transformer Bottleneck
articles.lede: The United States power grid has a supply problem measured in years: demand for transformers now runs 30% ahead of domestic production capacity, with lead times for large units approaching four years. At the center of the bottleneck is a single material — grain-oriented electrical steel — produced in North America by exactly one company, Cleveland-Cliffs.
articles.tweet_text: CLF – Cleveland-Cliffs Only North American producer of Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel, the material inside every transformer core in the US. US transformer lead times now 2 to 4 years. CLF is also building its own transformer plant in West Virginia, coming online this year.

articles.headline: Community Port Brings Meta's Vision Model to Apple Silicon in Real Time
articles.lede: A video posted by Maziyar Panahi shows traffic footage overlaid with segmentation masks — every car outlined, labeled, and confidence-scored — computed entirely on an M2 MacBook with no cloud connection. The model is Meta Platforms' SAM 3.1, officially shipped with server-GPU requirements; the Apple Silicon port is community work built on Apple's MLX framework. That the port exists, runs at video-ready speeds, and appeared within weeks of the server release marks a shift in how quickly AI research reaches consumer hardware.
articles.tweet_text: Wow! This is amazing! Segmented every car locally in real time with Meta's SAM3 converted to MLX. Just on-device (M2 laptop) vision getting absurdly good. Local AI is moving faster than most people realize! What other models should we test? what kind of videos?

articles.headline: Google's Midnight Globe Maps the World's 7,000 Languages
articles.lede: Language Explorer, a project from Google Research, is an interactive 3D globe that maps speaker counts, writing systems, and UNESCO endangerment status for more than 7,000 living languages. The poster @Aurelien_Gz holds it up as a masterclass in premium dark-mode web design — and the design awards agree. The more interesting story is what sits underneath the visual polish.

Built by the Wan-AI team at Alibaba Cloud, the series covers text-to-video, image-to-video, and a hybrid model in a unified framework. articles.lede: A cypherpunk's provocation cuts to the core of two cherished asset classes: gold bugs trust metal, Bitcoin maximalists trust mathematics — but both can be found, and what is found can be taken.

articles.headline: Why Today's S&P 500 Margins Dwarf the Dot-Com Era
articles.lede: A chart from BCA Research, circulating widely among macro traders in May 2026, shows S&P 500 net profit margins at their highest level in more than 15 years — roughly 13%, nearly double what prevailed at the peak of the dot-com bubble. Danish macro strategist Andreas Steno made the comparison explicit: this margin surge, he noted, did not happen ahead of the technology bust of 2000. Whether the difference is structural or cyclical is the live debate.

The mechanism turns out to be the alignment process itself.

articles.headline: The Arithmetic of Prediction: A Trader's Syllabus for Polymarket
articles.lede: Polymarket, the world's largest prediction market, rewards those who understand its underlying mathematics. A roadmap circulating on X distils the essential toolkit — from probability arithmetic to position sizing — into a syllabus any serious trader should absorb.
articles.tweet_text: Roan @RohOnChain The Math Needed for Trading on Polymarket (Complete Roadmap) 163 801 5.7K 3M I'm going to break down the essential math you need for trading on Polymarket. I'll also share the exact roadmap and resources that helped me personally. Let's get straight to it A recent research paper just exposed the reality. Sophisticated traders extracted $40 million in guaranteed arbitrage profits from Polymarket in one year. The top trader alone made $2,009,631.76. These aren't lucky gamblers. They're running Bregman projections, Frank-Wolfe algorithms, and solving optimization problems that would make most computer science PhDs uncomfortable. Bookmark This - I’m Roan, a backend developer working on system design, HFT-style execution, and quantitative trading systems. My work focuses on how prediction markets actually behave under load. When you see a market where YES is $0.62 and NO is $0.33, you think “that adds up to $0.95, there’s arbitrage.” You’re right. What most people never realize is that while they’re manually checking whether YES plus NO equals $1, quantitative systems are solving integer programs that scan 17,218 conditions across 2^63 possible outcomes in milliseconds. By the time a human places both orders, the spread is gone. The systems have already found the same violation across dozens of correlated markets, calculated optimal position sizes accounting for order book depth and fees, executed parallel non-atomic trades, and rotated capital into the next opportunity. The difference isn't just speed. It's mathematical infrastructure. By the end of this article, you will understand the exact optimization frameworks that extracted $40 million from Polymarket. You'll know why simple addition fails, how integer programming compresses exponential search spaces, and what Bregman divergence actually means for pricing efficiency. More importantly, you'll see the specific code patterns and algorithmic strategies that separate hobby projects from production systems running millions in capital. Note: This isn’t a skim. If you’re serious about building systems that can scale to seven figures, read it end to end. If you’re here for quick wins or vibe coding, this isn’t for you. Part I: The Marginal Polytope Problem (Why Simple Math Fails) The Reality of Multi-Condition Markets Single condition market: "Will Trump win Pennsylvania?" YES: $0.48 NO: $0.52 Sum: $1.00 Looks perfect. No arbitrage, right? Wrong. Now add another market: "Will Republicans win Pennsylvania by 5+ points?" YES: $0.32 NO: $0.68 Still both sum to $1. Still looks fine. But there's a logical dependency. If Republicans win by 5+ points, Trump must win Pennsylvania. These markets aren't independent. And that creates arbitrage. The Mathematical Framework For any market with n conditions, there are 2^n possible price combinations. But only n valid outcomes because exactly one condition must resolve to TRUE. Define the set of valid payoff vectors: Z = {φ(ω) : ω ∈ Ω} Where φ(ω) is a binary vector showing which condition is TRUE in outcome ω. The marginal polytope is the convex hull of these valid vectors: M = conv(Z) Arbitrage-free prices must lie in M. Anything outside M is exploitable. For the Pennsylvania example: Market A has 2 conditions, 2 valid outcomes Market B has 2 conditions, 2 valid outcomes Combined naive check: 2 × 2 = 4 possible outcomes Actual valid outcomes: 3 (dependency eliminates one) When prices assume 4 independent outcomes but only 3 exist, the mispricing creates guaranteed profit. Why Brute Force Dies NCAA 2010 tournament market had: 63 games (win/loss each) 2^63 = 9,223,372,036,854,775,808 possible outcomes 5,000+ securities Checking every combination is computationally impossible. The research paper found 1,576 potentially dependent market pairs in the 2024 US election alone. Naive pairwise verification would require checking 2^(n+m) combinations for each pair. At just 10 conditions per market, that's 2^20 = 1,048,576 checks per pair. Multiply by 1,576 pairs. Your laptop will still be computing when the election results are already known. The Integer Programming Solution Instead of enumerating outcomes, describe the valid set with linear constraints. Z = {z ∈ {0,1}^I : A^T × z ≥ b} Real example from Duke vs Cornell market: Each team has 7 securities (0 to 6 wins). That's 14 conditions, 2^14 = 16,384 possible combinations. But they can't both win 5+ games because they'd meet in the semifinals. Integer programming constraints: Sum of z(duke, 0 to 6) = 1 Sum of z(cornell, 0 to 6) = 1 z(duke,5) + z(duke,6) + z(cornell,5) + z(cornell,6) ≤ 1 Three linear constraints replace 16,384 brute force checks. This is how quantitative systems handle exponential complexity. They don't enumerate. They constrain. Detection Results from Real Data The research team analyzed markets from April 2024 to April 2025: 17,218 total conditions examined 7,051 conditions showed single-market arbitrage (41%) Median mispricing: $0.60 per dollar (should be $1.00) 13 confirmed dependent market pairs with exploitable arbitrage The median mispricing of $0.60 means markets were regularly wrong by 40%. Not close to efficient. Massively exploitable. Key takeaway: Arbitrage detection isn't about checking if numbers add up. It's about solving constraint satisfaction problems over exponentially large outcome spaces using compact linear representations. Part II: Bregman Projection (How to Actually Remove Arbitrage) Finding arbitrage is one problem. Calculating the optimal exploiting trade is another. You can't just "fix" prices by averaging or nudging numbers. You need to project the current market state onto the arbitrage-free manifold while preserving the information structure. Why Standard Distance Fails Euclidean projection would minimize: ||μ - θ||^2 This treats all price movements equally. But markets use cost functions. A price move from $0.50 to $0.60 has different information content than a move from $0.05 to $0.15, even though both are 10 cent changes. Market makers use logarithmic cost functions (LMSR) where prices represent implied probabilities. The right distance metric must respect this structure. The Bregman Divergence For any convex function R with gradient ∇R, the Bregman divergence is: D(μ||θ) = R(μ) + C(θ) - θ·μ Where: R(μ) is the convex conjugate of the cost function C θ is the current market state μ is the target price vector C(θ) is the market maker's cost function For LMSR, R(μ) is negative entropy: R(μ) = Sum of μ_i × ln(μ_i) This makes D(μ||θ) the Kullback-Leibler divergence, measuring information-theoretic distance between probability distributions. The Arbitrage Profit Formula The maximum guaranteed profit from any trade equals: max over all trades δ of [min over outcomes ω of (δ·φ(ω) - C(θ+δ) + C(θ))] = D(μ||θ)* Where μ* is the Bregman projection of θ onto M. This is not obvious. The proof requires convex duality theory. But the implication is clear: finding the optimal arbitrage trade is equivalent to computing the Bregman projection. Real Numbers The top arbitrageur extracted $2,009,631.76 over one year. Their strategy was solving this optimization problem faster and more accurately than everyone else: μ = argmin over μ in M of D(μ||θ)* Every profitable trade was finding μ* before prices moved. Why This Matters for Execution When you detect arbitrage, you need to know: What positions to take (which conditions to buy/sell) What size (accounting for order book depth) What profit to expect (accounting for execution risk) Bregman projection gives you all three. The projection μ* tells you the arbitrage-free price vector. The divergence D(μ*||θ) tells you the maximum extractable profit. The gradient ∇D tells you the trading direction. Without this framework, you're guessing. With it, you're optimizing. Key takeaway: Arbitrage isn't about spotting mispriced assets. It's about solving constrained convex optimization problems in spaces defined by market microstructure. The math determines profitability. You can't just "fix" prices by averaging or nudging numbers. You need to project the current market state onto the arbitrage-free manifold while preserving the information structure. Part III: The Frank-Wolfe Algorithm (Making It Computationally Tractable) Computing the Bregman projection directly is intractable. The marginal polytope M has exponentially many vertices. Standard convex optimization requires access to the full constraint set. For prediction markets, that means enumerating every valid outcome. Impossible at scale. The Frank-Wolfe algorithm solves this by reducing projection to a sequence of linear programs. The Core Insight Instead of optimizing over all of M at once, Frank-Wolfe builds it iteratively. Algorithm: 1. Start with a small set of known vertices Z_0 2. For iteration t: a. Solve convex optimization over conv(Z_{t-1}) μ_t = argmin over μ in conv(Z_{t-1}) of F(μ) b. Find new descent vertex by solving IP: z_t = argmin over z in Z of ∇F(μ_t)·z c. Add to active set: Z_t = Z_{t-1} ∪ {z_t} d. Compute convergence gap: g(μ_t) = ∇F(μ_t)·(μ_t - z_t) e. Stop if g(μ_t) ≤ ε The active set Z_t grows by one vertex per iteration. Even after 100 iterations, you're only tracking 100 vertices instead of 2^63. The Integer Programming Oracle Step 2b is the expensive part. Each iteration requires solving: min over z in Z of c·z Where c = ∇F(μ_t) is the current gradient and Z is the set of valid payoff vectors defined by integer constraints. This is an integer linear program. NP-hard in general. But modern IP solvers like Gurobi handle these efficiently for well-structured problems. The research team used Gurobi 5.5. Typical solve times: Early iterations (small partial outcomes): under 1 second Mid-tournament (30-40 games settled): 10-30 seconds Late tournament (50+ games settled): under 5 seconds Why does it get faster later? Because as outcomes settle, the feasible set shrinks. Fewer variables, tighter constraints, faster solves. The Controlled Growth Problem Standard Frank-Wolfe assumes the gradient ∇F is Lipschitz continuous with bounded constant. For LMSR, ∇R(μ) = ln(μ) + 1. As μ approaches 0, the gradient explodes to negative infinity. This violates standard convergence proofs. The solution is Barrier Frank-Wolfe. Instead of optimizing over M, optimize over a contracted polytope: M' = (1-ε)M + εu Where u is an interior point with all coordinates strictly between 0 and 1, and ε in (0,1) is the contraction parameter. For any ε greater than 0, the gradient is bounded on M'. The Lipschitz constant is O(1/ε). The algorithm adaptively decreases ε as iterations progress: If g(μ_t) / (-4g_u) < ε_{t-1}: ε_t = min{g(μ_t)/(-4g_u), ε_{t-1}/2} Else: ε_t = ε_{t-1} This ensures ε goes to 0 asymptotically, so the contracted problem converges to the true projection. Convergence Rate Frank-Wolfe converges at rate O(L × diam(M) / t) where L is the Lipschitz constant and diam(M) is the diameter of M. For LMSR with adaptive contraction, this becomes O(1/(ε×t)). As ε shrinks adaptively, convergence slows but remains polynomial. The research showed that in practice, 50 to 150 iterations were sufficient for convergence on markets with thousands of conditions. Production Performance From the paper: "Once projections become practically fast, FWMM achieves superior accuracy to LCMM." Timeline: First 16 games: LCMM and FWMM perform similarly (IP solver too slow) After 45 games settled: First successful 30-minute projection completes Remaining tournament: FWMM outperforms LCMM by 38% median improvement on security prices The crossover point is when the outcome space shrinks enough for IP solves to complete within trading timeframes. Key takeaway: Theoretical elegance means nothing without computational tractability. Frank-Wolfe with integer programming oracles makes Bregman projection practical on markets with trillions of outcomes. This is how $40 million in arbitrage actually got computed and executed. Part IV: Execution Under Non-Atomic Constraints (Why Order Books Change Everything) You've detected arbitrage. You've computed the optimal trade via Bregman projection. Now you need to execute. This is where most strategies fail. The Non-Atomic Problem Polymarket uses a Central Limit Order Book (CLOB). Unlike decentralized exchanges where arbitrage can be atomic (all trades succeed or all fail), CLOB execution is sequential. Your arbitrage plan: Buy YES at $0.30 Buy NO at $0.30 Total cost: $0.60 Guaranteed payout: $1.00 Expected profit: $0.40 Reality: Submit YES order → Fills at $0.30 ✓ Price updates due to your order Submit NO order → Fills at $0.78 ✗ Total cost: $1.08 Payout: $1.00 Actual result: -$0.08 loss One leg fills. The other doesn't. You're exposed. This is why the research paper only counted opportunities with at least $0.05 profit margin. Smaller edges get eaten by execution risk. Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) Analysis Instead of assuming instant fills at quoted prices, calculate expected execution price: VWAP = Sum of (price_i × volume_i) / Sum of (volume_i) The research methodology: For each block on Polygon (approximately 2 seconds): Calculate VWAP_yes from all YES trades in that block Calculate VWAP_no from all NO trades in that block If abs(VWAP_yes + VWAP_no - 1.0) > 0.02: Record arbitrage opportunity Profit = abs(VWAP_yes + VWAP_no - 1.0) Blocks are the atomic time unit. Analyzing per-block VWAP captures the actual achievable prices, not the fantasy of instant execution. The Liquidity Constraint Even if prices are mispriced, you can only capture profit up to available liquidity. Real example from the data: Market shows arbitrage: sum of YES prices = $0.85 Potential profit: $0.15 per dollar Order book depth at these prices: $234 total volume Maximum extractable profit: $234 × 0.15 = $35.10 The research calculated maximum profit per opportunity as: profit = (price deviation) × min(volume across all required positions) For multi-condition markets, you need liquidity in ALL positions simultaneously. The minimum determines your cap. Time Window Analysis The research used a 950-block window (approximately 1 hour) to group related trades. Why 1 hour? Because 75% of matched orders on Polymarket fill within this timeframe. Orders submitted, matched, and executed on-chain typically complete within 60 minutes. For each trader address, all bids within a 950-block window were grouped as a single strategy execution. Profit was calculated as the guaranteed minimum payout across all possible outcomes minus total cost. Execution Success Rate Of the detected arbitrage opportunities: Single condition arbitrage: 41% of conditions had opportunities, most were exploited Market rebalancing: 42% of multi-condition markets had opportunities Combinatorial arbitrage: 13 valid pairs identified, 5 showed execution The gap between detection and execution is execution risk. Latency Layers: The Speed Hierarchy Retail trader execution: Polymarket API call: ~50ms Matching engine: ~100ms Polygon block time: ~2,000ms Block propagation: ~500ms Total: ~2,650ms Sophisticated arbitrage system: WebSocket price feed: <5ms (real-time push) Decision computation: <10ms (pre-calculated) Direct RPC submission: ~15ms (bypass API) Parallel execution: ~10ms (all legs at once) Polygon block inclusion: ~2,000ms (unavoidable) Total: ~2,040ms The 20-30ms you see on-chain is decision-to-mempool time. Fast wallets submit all positions within 30ms, eliminating sequential execution risk by confirming everything in the same block. The compounding advantage: By the time you see their transaction confirmed on-chain (Block N), they detected the opportunity 2+ seconds earlier (Block N-1), submitted all legs in 30ms, and the market already rebalanced. When you copy at Block N+1, you're 4 seconds behind a sub-second opportunity. Why Copytrading Fast Wallets Fails What actually happens: Block N-1: Fast system detects mispricing, submits 4 transactions in 30ms Block N: All transactions confirm, arbitrage captured, you see this Block N+1: You copy their trade, but price is now $0.78 (was $0.30) You're not arbitraging. You're providing exit liquidity. Order book depth kills you: Fast wallet buys 50,000 tokens: VWAP: $0.322 across multiple price levels Market moves You buy 5,000 tokens after: VWAP: $0.344 (market already shifted) They paid $0.322, you paid $0.344 Their 10 cent edge became your 2.2 cent loss The Capital Efficiency Problem Top arbitrageur operated with $500K+ capital. With $5K capital, the same strategy breaks because: Slippage eats larger percentage of smaller positions Cannot diversify across enough opportunities Single failed execution wipes out days of profit Fixed costs (gas) consume more of profit margin Gas fees on 4-leg strategy: ~$0.02 $0.08 profit → 25% goes to gas $0.03 profit → 67% goes to gas This is why $0.05 minimum threshold exists. Real Execution Data Single condition arbitrage: Detected: 7,051 conditions Executed: 87% success rate Failed due to: liquidity (48%), price movement (31%), competition (21%) Combinatorial arbitrage: Detected: 13 pairs Executed: 45% success rate Failed due to: insufficient simultaneous liquidity (71%), speed competition (18%) Key takeaway: Mathematical correctness is necessary but not sufficient. Execution speed, order book depth, and non-atomic fill risk determine actual profitability. The research showed $40 million extracted because sophisticated actors solved execution problems, not just math problems. Part V: The Complete System (What Actually Got Deployed) Theory is clean. Production is messy. Here's what a working arbitrage system actually looks like based on the research findings and practical requirements. The Data Pipeline Real-time requirements: WebSocket connection to Polymarket CLOB API └─ Order book updates (price/volume changes) └─ Trade execution feed (fills happening) └─ Market creation/settlement events Historical analysis: Alchemy Polygon node API └─ Query events from contract 0x4D97DCd97eC945f40cF65F87097ACe5EA0476045 └─ OrderFilled events (trades executed) └─ PositionSplit events (new tokens minted) └─ PositionsMerge events (tokens burned) The research analyzed 86 million transactions. That volume requires infrastructure, not scripts. The Dependency Detection Layer For 305 US election markets, there are 46,360 possible pairs to check. Manual analysis is impossible. The research used DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B with prompt engineering: Input: Two markets with their condition descriptions Output: JSON of valid outcome combinations Validation checks: 1. Does each market have exactly one TRUE condition per outcome? 2. Are there fewer valid combinations than n × m (dependency exists)? 3. Do dependent subsets satisfy arbitrage conditions? Results on election markets: 40,057 independent pairs (no arbitrage possible) 1,576 dependent pairs (potential arbitrage) 374 satisfied strict combinatorial conditions 13 manually verified as exploitable 81.45% accuracy on complex multi-condition markets. Good enough for filtering. Requires manual verification for execution. The Optimization Engine Three-layer arbitrage removal: Layer 1: Simple LCMM constraints Fast linear programming relaxations. Check basic constraints like "sum of probabilities equals 1" and "if A implies B, then P(A) cannot exceed P(B)." Runs in milliseconds. Removes obvious mispricing. Layer 2: Integer programming projection Frank-Wolfe algorithm with Gurobi IP solver. Parameters from research: Alpha = 0.9 (extract at least 90% of available arbitrage) Initial epsilon = 0.1 (10% contraction) Convergence threshold = 1e-6 Time limit = 30 minutes (reduced as markets shrink) Typical iterations: 50 to 150. Typical solve time per iteration: 1 to 30 seconds depending on market size. Layer 3: Execution validation Before submitting orders, simulate fills against current order book. Check: Is liquidity sufficient at these prices? What is expected slippage? What is guaranteed profit after slippage? Does profit exceed minimum threshold (research used $0.05)? Only execute if all checks pass. Position Sizing Logic Modified Kelly criterion accounting for execution risk: f = (b×p - q) / b × sqrt(p)* Where: b = arbitrage profit percentage p = probability of full execution (estimated from order book depth) q = 1 - p Cap at 50% of order book depth to avoid moving the market. The Monitoring Dashboard Track in real-time: Opportunities detected per minute Opportunities executed per minute Execution success rate Total profit (running sum) Current drawdown percentage Average latency (detection to submission) Alerts: Drawdown exceeds 15% Execution rate drops below 30% IP solver timeouts increase Order fill failures spike The research identified the top arbitrageur made 4,049 transactions. That's approximately 11 trades per day over one year. Not high-frequency in the traditional sense, but systematic and consistent. The Actual Results Total extracted April 2024 to April 2025: Single condition arbitrage: Buy both < $1: $5,899,287 Sell both > $1: $4,682,075 Subtotal: $10,581,362 Market rebalancing: Buy all YES < $1: $11,092,286 Sell all YES > $1: $612,189 Buy all NO: $17,307,114 Subtotal: $29,011,589 Combinatorial arbitrage: Cross-market execution: $95,634 Total: $39,688,585 Top 10 extractors took $8,127,849 (20.5% of total). Top single extractor: $2,009,632 from 4,049 trades. Average profit per trade for top player: $496. Not lottery wins. Not lucky timing. Mathematical precision executed systematically. What Separates Winners from Losers The research makes it clear: Retail approach: Check prices every 30 seconds See if YES + NO roughly equals $1 Maybe use a spreadsheet Manual order submission Hope for the best Quantitative approach: Real-time WebSocket feeds Integer programming for dependency detection Frank-Wolfe with Bregman projection for optimal trades Parallel order execution with VWAP estimation Systematic position sizing under execution constraints 2.65 second latency vs. 30 second polling One group extracted $40 million. The other group provided the liquidity. Key takeaway: Production systems require mathematical rigor AND engineering sophistication. Optimization theory, distributed systems, real-time data processing, risk management, execution algorithms. All of it. The math is the foundation. The infrastructure is what makes it profitable. The Final Reality While traders were reading "10 tips for prediction markets," quantitative systems were: Solving integer programs to detect dependencies across 17,218 conditions Computing Bregman projections to find optimal arbitrage trades Running Frank-Wolfe algorithms with controlled gradient growth Executing parallel orders with VWAP-based slippage estimation Systematically extracting $40 million in guaranteed profits The difference is not luck. It's mathematical infrastructure. The research paper is public. The algorithms are known. The profits are real. The question is: can you build it before the next $40 million is extracted? Resources: Research paper: "Unravelling the Probabilistic Forest: Arbitrage in Prediction Markets" (arXiv:2508.03474v1) Theory foundation: "Arbitrage-Free Combinatorial Market Making via Integer Programming" (arXiv:1606.02825v2) IP solver: Gurobi Optimizer LLM for dependencies: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B Data source: Alchemy Polygon node API The math works. articles.headline: Beijing Student's Agent Engine Tops GitHub and Spawns a DeFi Fork
articles.lede: Guo Hangjiang, a 20-year-old undergraduate at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, built a multi-agent social simulation tool called MiroFish in ten days and watched it reach number one on GitHub's global trending list. Hot growth stocks attract substantial interest from investors; however, future stock market winners are
difficult to identify using traditional metrics of fundamental analysis (such as cash flow, profitability or
earnings per share). This study investigates the characteristics of "multibagger stocks" - stocks that increase
in value several times the original investment - and detects key drivers of their abnormal investment returns.
An empirical analysis of 464 multibagger stocks listed on major American stock exchanges, cach increasing
in value by at least tenfold during 2009-2024, was conducted. A dynamic panel data model was developed
to explain the sources of their outperformance and to predict future returs. The findings indicate that
several traditional Fama-French factors, including size, value and profitability, remain significant predictors
of future multibagger returs: small-cap high-value high-profitability stocks outperform. Additionally, the
analysis identifies further important drivers of multibagger stock outperformance. These include
fundamental, technical, and macrocconomic variables, such as high free cash flow yield, distinctive
investment patterns linked to EBITDA growth, complex momentum effects with quick trend reversals that
limit optimal entry points, and specific interest rate environment.
This study advances asset pricing research by developing a novel, empirically validated model to explain
the multibagger phenomenon. It offers valuable practical insights for investors and asset managers and
provides a robust theoretical foundation for future stock screening strategies aimed at identifying potential
multibazeers and maximising canital gains.

articles.headline: The Competitor List Is the Research: What Coherent's 10-K Reveals About the Next Wave of Photonics Winners
articles.lede: For years, a quiet corner of public disclosure has done the work most investors outsource to expensive sell-side analysts: the competitor table buried deep in a large-cap's annual SEC filing. A single such list from Coherent Corp.'s 2022 10-K named, among others, a Canadian specialty-materials firm then trading below a dollar that has since risen more than thirty-fold.
articles.tweet_text: Fun fact for research: You can find a lot of "hidden gems" by looking at who companies like $COHR lists as competitors in the SEC filings. Names I've mentioned like 5N are there and it went from $.92 -> $24 in a few years. $LITE , Eoptolink, Innolight, are all there too. This was year 2022. A lot of them turn out really well in a few years.

articles.headline: S&P 500 Call-Options Frenzy Echoes Classic Blow-Off Top Patterns
articles.lede: Grok, xAI’s AI market commentator, flagged in May 2026 that current S&P 500 options activity carries the hallmarks of the speculative frenzies that preceded the crashes of 1929, 2000, and 2021. The immediate catalyst: on May 7–8, S&P 500 call options traded a notional $2.6 trillion in a single session—an all-time record in U.S. market history. Entered into a ZeroHedge-adjacent thread, the reply synthesises historical pattern recognition with a pointed warning about current market structure.
articles.tweet_text: Not always, but yes—many major market tops (esp. parabolic ones) feature explosive volume in the final "blow-off" phase as euphoria draws in late buyers. Classic examples include 1929, 2000 dot-com, and 2021 meme surges. That said, volume often peaks *before* the actual high as distribution begins, with downside confirmation via selling spikes or divergences. High call skew like now signals similar frenzy—watch SPX volume and breadth closely.

articles.lede: A post by @parmita argues that the steady drip of pop-psychology content on TikTok has displaced something more fundamental: a working understanding of how the brain actually operates. The claim is that concepts like the default mode network and the prefrontal cortex belong in general literacy, not graduate seminars. The underlying diagnosis has real empirical support.

articles.headline: The Next Leg of the AI Trade May Run on Electricity, Not Silicon
articles.lede: As semiconductor stocks have surged on AI infrastructure buildout, a quieter beneficiary has barely moved: independent power producers sitting on fleets of dispatchable, always-on generation that hyperscalers increasingly cannot find anywhere else. With GE Vernova up roughly 280% from its 2024 lows and Bloom Energy up more than 2,000% from its 2025 trough, Vistra Corp. — at $161, still a third below its late-2025 peak — looks like an overlooked node in the same circuit.
articles.tweet_text: As semis have gone parabolic, it's logical to think where the next run of this AI trade is going to occur. The next possible rotation sector of the AI trade is the independent power producers who have largely sat this run out. Independent Power Producers are well positioned to capitalize on the structural surge in U.S. power demand driven by AI data centers, electrification, and hyperscaler needs. I really like $VST here. With a ~20 GW fleet (nuclear, gas, battery storage) heavily concentrated in high growth markets like ERCOT and PJM, plus a contract heavy commercial strategy that bypasses traditional rate-base regulation, Vistra offers direct exposure to the AI power theme without the drag of being a regulated utility. With $GEV and $BE having already gone bananas, names like VST are probably due for a rotation soon. I don't expect parabolic moves, but I do think it's time for a long.

articles.headline: A Slim Guide Promises Math Fluency Without the Formulas
articles.lede: A user with a philosophy-of-physics bent shares the cover of Albert Rutherford's 2021 self-help primer, *Mathematical Thinking: For People Who Hate Math*. The book, 134 pages and marketed as an entry in an 'Advanced Thinking Skills' series, argues that most people's aversion to math is a pedagogical wound, not a cognitive one. Its pitch: the useful parts of mathematical reasoning — assessing risk, parsing probability, making better decisions — can be taught without demanding fluency in calculus or geometry.

articles.headline: Two Terminal Commands Unlock Faster Mac Keyboard Repeat Than Apple Allows
articles.lede: macOS ships keyboard-repeat settings capped well above their hardware minimum. Two `defaults write` commands reach below the System Settings slider floor — cutting the repeat interval to 15 milliseconds and the initial-hold delay to 150 milliseconds — without installing any software.
articles.tweet_text: If you own a Mac, do yourself a favor and run the following in a terminal: defaults write -g KeyRepeat -int 1 defaults write -g InitialKeyRepeat -int 10

articles.headline: Four Dimensions, Zero Plugins: Gaussian Splatting Hits the Browser
articles.lede: A clip circulating on X shows a photorealistic volumetric scene — a human figure in motion, captured simultaneously from a dome of cameras and rendered as a freely navigable world — playing back in real time inside an ordinary web browser. The interface labels “SCENE Fashion” and “ENVIRONMENT Street Dome” are consistent with 4DV.ai’s browser-native viewer, a Chinese platform built on PlayCanvas and the WebGPU rendering API that requires no download or install. Behind the impression of effortlessness lies a decade of compressive geometry research and two years of engineering to make GPU-side depth sorting viable in a consumer browser.
articles.tweet_text: 4D Gaussian Splatting is mindblowing. How is this level of fidelity and realism able to run so flawlessly on a web browser?

articles.headline: When Anyone Can Build Software, Only Sales Still Pays
articles.lede: A short thread opening from @boneGPT crystallizes an argument spreading quietly through startup circles: that AI-assisted coding has hollowed out the engineering advantage so thoroughly that distribution and sales are now the only durable edges left. The claim is sweeping, partly right, and worth taking seriously even where it overshoots.

articles.headline: Charcuterie Maps Unicode's 160,000 Characters by Visual Shape
articles.lede: Unicode 17.0 defines nearly 160,000 assigned characters — each catalogued by name, script, block, and codepoint. Every existing browser for the standard organizes them by that taxonomy, which is useful for engineers but maddening for anyone who knows what a character looks like but cannot name it. Charcuterie, built by Zürich-based interaction developer David Aerne, inverts the interface: choose a glyph, and the tool returns everything in the standard that looks like it.

articles.headline: The Map That Black-Scholes Cannot Draw
articles.lede: A NASA physicist turned quant has published a preprint arguing that the most famous formula in finance is not wrong so much as incomplete — the flat-space special case of a richer geometry, one whose curvature is precisely what options markets have been pricing all along.
articles.tweet_text: Black-Scholes is wrong almost everywhere. And yet, it’s still the language of options markets. The reason: It’s the flat limit of a curved geometric pricing space. The volatility smile? That’s the curvature. Below we see where markets actually live in that space Preprint: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6630259…

articles.headline: A Real Defence AI Hardware Story, Dressed in SaaS Metrics
articles.lede: One Stop Systems (OSS) — a small-cap maker of ruggedised AI compute hardware for military and industrial applications — surged 57% in a single session on May 6, 2026, after reporting first-quarter results that matched the tweet's figures almost to the decimal. The real story is a genuine operational transformation: OSS shed a low-margin European distribution subsidiary in late 2025 and re-emerged as a focused defence AI hardware manufacturer with sharply improved unit economics. Several of the framing choices, however — a software valuation metric applied to a hardware business, a "near monopoly" claim in a market with real rivals, and a single-quarter snapshot presented as a sustained trend — call for scrutiny.

articles.headline: Corporate Profits Near Post-War Highs Signal an Equity Melt-Up
articles.lede: A FRED chart tracking the corporate profit share of America's gross domestic income against the labor compensation share over seven decades forms the empirical backbone of a bullish equity call. The two series — profits near their post-World War II ceiling, workers' wages near a multi-decade floor — point, in the analyst's reading, to conditions ripe for a rapid melt-up in equity prices. The argument rests not on sentiment alone but on a macroeconomic accounting identity that links government deficits directly to corporate earnings.

articles.headline: Scripture's Angels Bear No Resemblance to Popular Iconography
articles.lede: The tweet from @MatrixMysteries launches a thread on what the Bible actually says about angels — a subject where popular imagination has drifted almost completely from the source texts. In canonical Scripture, angels do not resemble gentle, feathered humanoids. They appear as fiery, multi-faced, many-eyed entities whose proximity causes physical prostration, and their first words to humans are almost invariably a command to stop being terrified.
articles.tweet_text: This is what angels look like according to the Bible. A thread explaining the 9 types of angels — and why they always say: “Do not be afraid...”

articles.headline: Mapping the Gap in Claude's Research Workflow
articles.lede: A product designer's “what if” post sketches a two-pane Claude interface where research findings flow into a visual canvas rather than a prose report. The image is almost certainly a concept mockup — Claude does not yet ship this feature — but it names a real and acknowledged gap in how the model presents knowledge. The observation arrives as a growing category of AI mind-mapping tools fills exactly that space.

articles.headline: A Famous Maxim, an Unverified Source, and a Useful Idea
articles.lede: A quote attributed to Charlie Munger — buy quality stocks on the 200-week moving average and beat the market — has spread across financial social media with the velocity of gospel. The idea is sound enough; the attribution is shakier than its fans acknowledge.
articles.tweet_text: "If all you ever did was buy high-quality stocks on the 200-week moving average, you would beat the S&P 500 by a large margin over time." -Charlie Munger

articles.headline: Japan's Digital-Twin Commission Preempted a Commercial Three.js Sky System
articles.lede: Dan Greenheck, a Three.js educator who sells commercial WebGL add-ons, was midway through building Three.js Sky Pro — a paid atmosphere-and-clouds package — when he discovered that a Tokyo design consultancy had already released the same thing, more capable, under an MIT licence, for free. The library is @takram/three-geospatial, and its existence is almost perfectly ironic: it is a side effect of a Japanese government contract, published when that engagement ended.
articles.tweet_text: Well this is a bit of a bummer. I discovered there's an existing free atmosphere/cloud package for Three.js / R3F that has all the features I was planning on implementing for Three.js Sky Pro. The weird thing is I knew this existed already? But when I searched for it, I think I happened across a different, less-featured solution. I guess it's back to the drawing board!

articles.headline: Richard Hamming's Prescription for Doing Work That Matters
articles.lede: The occasion is casual — a book stolen from a friend, not coming back. Richard Hamming's *The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn* began as thirty lectures at the Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey during the 1990s, was published in 1997, and spent two decades in relative obscurity before Stripe reissued it in 2020. Hamming himself spent thirty years at Bell Telephone Laboratories, won the 1968 ACM Turing Award, and gave his name to the error-correcting codes that underpin virtually every digital communications system.
articles.tweet_text: Stole a book from a friend. Oops. not giving it back.

articles.headline: The Tolstoy Gateway That Fits in an Afternoon
articles.lede: Leo Tolstoy's reputation rests on doorstoppers — *War and Peace* runs to 1,300 pages and has been intimidating readers since 1869. But Tolstoy also wrote *The Death of Ivan Ilyich*, a novella of roughly 100 pages that distils his moral and spiritual concerns into a form anyone can finish in a sitting. The recommendation to start there is old advice, and it remains sound.
articles.tweet_text: If you want to start reading Tolstoy, start with The Death of Ivan Ilyich. Deep. Meaningful. Thought provoking. Only ~100 pages. You can read it in an afternoon and it will stick with you for a lifetime.

articles.headline: A Patent Licensor's Gains Are the Market's Work, Not Its Own
articles.lede: Adeia (ADEA), a pure-play intellectual-property licensing company, returned 33% over the past 30 days — yet a quantitative return-attribution dashboard shows the company's own fundamentals subtracted value over that stretch. @tomhou101 is responding to @pennycheck with a pointed observation: how much of the gain belongs to Adeia's specific story, and how much is the stock simply being carried by macro and sector tailwinds?
articles.tweet_text: Look at stock attribution. Like you said: currently fundamentals attributing negatively, so market isn't pricing in any idiosyncratic returns for it. If this changes, could be a sign that markets are starting to re-price. Better not to fight markets until they change their mind?

articles.headline: Boethius's Musical Mathematics and the 432 Hz Myth
articles.lede: Written around 510 CE by a Roman senator awaiting execution, *De institutione musica* shaped Western music education for nearly nine centuries. Its author, Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, transmitted ancient Greek mathematical philosophy about music — he did not discover it — and the work makes no claims about specific frequencies, since the hertz as a unit would not exist for fourteen more centuries. A contemporary account attaches a sacred-geometry frequency diagram to Boethius's legacy and presents both as suppressed cosmic knowledge.
articles.tweet_text: Some of the most important things a child can learn are no longer taught in school. That is why parents and children should follow Beyond the Cosmic Veil.

articles.headline: How to Prompt a Human: An Autistic Theory of Social Fluency
articles.lede: A Twitter thread by @DefenderOfBasic argues that autistic people struggle socially not because they lack rules, but because the layer of rules they've studied is the wrong one. The proposed fix is to treat social interaction as a developer treats a language model: prompt, observe, predict, iterate. The metaphor turns out to have sharper academic backing than its self-help framing suggests.

articles.headline: A 12-Megabyte Go Binary Takes Aim at Browser Control for AI Agents
articles.lede: AI agents that must navigate the web have long faced a choice between heavyweight automation frameworks and expensive screenshot-based vision. Pinchtab, released in February 2026 by UK developer Luigi Agosti, proposes a third path: a single self-contained binary exposing Chrome browser control through a plain HTTP API, with no runtime dependencies and no framework allegiance. Three months in, it has attracted nearly 9,000 GitHub stars and a growing ecosystem of third-party integrations.
articles.tweet_text: Someone just solved the biggest bottleneck in AI agents. And it's a 12MB binary. It's called Pinchtab. It gives any AI agent full browser control through a plain HTTP API. Not locked to a framework. Not tied to an SDK. Any agent, any language, even curl. No config. No setup. No dependencies. Just a single Go binary. Here's why every existing solution is broken: → OpenClaw's browser? Only works inside OpenClaw → Playwright MCP? Framework-locked → Browser Use? Coupled to its own stack Pinchtab is a standalone HTTP server. Your agent sends HTTP requests. That's it. Here's what this thing does: → Launches and manages its own Chrome instances → Exposes an accessibility-first DOM tree with stable element refs → Click, type, scroll, navigate. All via simple HTTP calls → Built-in stealth mode that bypasses bot detection on major sites → Persistent sessions. Log in once, stays logged in across restarts → Multi-instance orchestration with a real-time dashboard → Works headless or headed (human does 2FA, agent takes over) Here's the wildest part: A full page snapshot costs ~800 tokens with Pinchtab's /text endpoint. The same page via screenshots? ~10,000 tokens. That's 13x cheaper. On a 50-page monitoring task, you're paying $0.01 instead of $0.30. It even has smart diff mode. Only returns what changed since the last snapshot. Your agent stops re-reading the entire page every single call. 1.6K GitHub stars. 478 commits. 15 releases. Actively maintained. 100% Open Source. MIT License.

articles.headline: Norway's Wealth Tax Sent the Rich Packing to Switzerland
articles.lede: When Norway's Labour government raised the wealth tax to 1.1 percent in 2022, it expected extra revenue. It got a different result: a historic exodus of the country's richest citizens, most of them bound for the Swiss cantons of Zug and Lugano.
articles.tweet_text: The crazy story of how Norway gifted 5,000 millionaires and $100s of billions to Switzerlandin just 2 years: In 2022, Norway raised its wealth tax to 1.1% (highest in Europe) and its capital gains tax to 38% (2nd highest). It made it virtually impossible to preserve wealth in the country and forced Norwegian millionaires out of the country. Here's how: If you have $100m in taxable wealth (to pick a round number), you need to pay $1.1 million in wealth tax each year. But where do you find that $1.1 million? Well, you have to sell off assets. But if you sell $1.1 million of assets, this triggers a 38% capital gains tax, leaving you with just $682k (not enough to pay the wealth tax). So you have to sell MORE assets. To pay both the wealth tax AND the capital gains tax on the money you were forced to raise, you actually have to sell assets worth closer to $1.8 million. Then you need to pay the entire $1.8m to the government - JUST TO KEEP THE MONEY YOU ALREADY PAID TAX ON WHEN YOU MADE IT IN THE FIRST PLACE. In other words, if you do nothing, you lose 1/50th of your wealth every year. And this doesn't even account for inflation or bear market years. It often also means losing control of your company, since you have to sell shares every year. And if you're a startup unfortunate enough to get investment at a high valuation, you will have to borrow money just to pay tax on money you haven't even earned yet! So, 5,000 Norwegians understandably moved to Switzerland, including 500 of the richest people in the country. And the ones who didn't leave in time, hoping for cooler heads to prevail, got punished severely. Because when the government saw what was happening, they introduced an EXIT TAX (effectively a financial Berlin Wall). So now, if you want to leave Norway, you have to pay 38% of the market value of ALL YOUR ASSETS. And the worst part is that the Norwegian government doesn't even need this tax money in the slightest. Because thanks to enormous oil and gas revenue, only about 18% of the government's revenue comes from taxes paid by private citizens. And only a fraction of that from wealth tax. Norway also has the world's biggest sovereign wealth fund, today worth $1.6 TRILLION, or $320,000 per Norwegian. Even if Norway didn't collect a single dollar in tax, it could still fund government spending for a decade using the money in that fund. The Norwegian government does not need the money. It is simply greedy and spiteful. Why would anyone EVER build anything in Norway? This is how you destroy the private sector as fast as possible. I suspect this is what this government ultimately wants since they can then control the remaining population with handouts. Some loopholes still exist, but they are closing fast. If you're a Norwegian who wants to get out of this abusive relationship, let me know, and I will put you in touch with people who can help.

articles.headline: Flipbook Envisions a Web Built Entirely on AI-Generated Pixels
articles.lede: On April 23, 2026, a three-person team unveiled **Flipbook**, a prototype that discards the web's entire rendering stack—HTML, CSS, the layout engine—and replaces it with a generative video model that draws every visible pixel on demand. The result is an interface where clicking a landmark on a travel page reshapes the whole canvas into a new illustrated scene, with no underlying document model, no selectable text, and no fixed buttons. Whether this represents a glimpse of a post-browser future or a compelling dead end is the question it forces.

articles.headline: No Compromise Required: How Open Source Became a Game Engine Advantage
articles.lede: Will Eastcott helped build *RenderWare*, the PS2-era graphics middleware that powered the *Grand Theft Auto* series, before co-founding PlayCanvas — a WebGL game engine built natively for the browser and MIT-licensed since 2014. His assertion that open source has ceased to be a compromise is not promotional boilerplate; it is the conclusion of someone who watched a proprietary platform become a liability the moment its corporate owner's interests diverged from its users'. articles.headline: Sand.ai Bets a Single Attention Stream Can Unify Video and Speech
articles.lede: Most AI video models that attempt to synchronize speech and lip movement lean on complexity — separate audio and video branches, cross-attention fusion layers, post-hoc sync corrections. A model called daVinci-MagiHuman, released in March 2026 by the Beijing startup Sand.ai and the SII-GAIR Lab at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, bets on the opposite: that a single unified Transformer processing text, video, and audio as one token sequence will be simultaneously simpler, faster, and better. Its release under Apache 2.0 — with full weights and inference code — puts the architecture in anyone's hands.
articles.tweet_text: BREAKING: A research lab just released a 15B model that generates multilingual talking human videos with synced audio, beats every competitor in human evaluation, and runs in 38 seconds on one GPU. It's called daVinci-MagiHuman. The key insight is that every other model in this category stacks cross-attention, multi-stream pipelines, and separate conditioning branches to handle video and audio together. This one throws all of that out and uses a single unified self-attention stream across all modalities. Super-resolution happens in latent space rather than pixel space so there's no extra VAE decode-encode round trip. The turbo VAE decoder cuts decoding overhead even further. The distilled version runs in 8 steps with no CFG at all. Visual quality, text alignment, and word error rate all beat Ovi 1.1 and LTX 2.3 on the benchmark table. 100% Opensource. Apache 2.0. Repo and research paper links are in the comments.

Its author, Baron Frédéric de Portal, argued that every ancient civilization shared a symbolic language written in colour — and that the moment God divided light from darkness was its generative first word. The image is not decoration; it is a thesis.

articles.headline: Sabi's Mind-Reading Beanie Promises Thought-to-Text Without Surgery
articles.lede: A California startup called Sabi wants to make the surgeon optional. Its product, the Sabi Cap, is a knitted beanie lined with up to 100,000 custom biosensors that record the brain's electrical activity through the scalp — no incision, no implant. The company claims its artificial-intelligence system can translate *internal speech* into typed text at roughly 30 words per minute, a figure that, if verified, would exceed anything demonstrated in the peer-reviewed literature.
articles.tweet_text: This is the AlphaFold moment for brain-computer interfaces. Sabi releases the Sabi Cap. The first mass BCI (brain-computer interfaces) may be something you wear, not something surgeons implant. It is a normal beanie you wear on your head. Inside sit 70,000 to 100,000 tiny custom biosensors that read electrical signals from your brain through your scalp. They trained a Brain Foundation Model on 100,000 hours of neural data from 100 people. The model turns your internal speech into text on a computer screen. You think the words and it types them at about 30 words per minute right now. You also click, select, or command software purely by intending the action. “The biggest and baddest application of BCI is if you can talk to your computer by thinking about it,” says Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, one of Sabi’s investors. “If you're going to have a billion people use BCI for access to their computers every day, it can't be invasive.” Sabi’s mind-reading hat uses Electroencephalography, or EEG, which records the brain’s electrical activity through metal discs placed on the scalp. The downside of traditional wearable system is that its sensors have to detect brain activity through skin and bone, which weakens the signals. Surgically implanted devices capture much stronger signals because they sit much closer to neurons. Sabi believes the way to improve accuracy in a wearable is to massively increase the number of sensors. Most Electroencephalography devices use anywhere from 12 to a few 100 sensors. Sabi’s cap is expected to use around 70,000 to 100,000 tiny sensors.

articles.headline: Among AI's Builders, AGI Has Become a Matter of Faith
articles.lede: Karen Hao, a journalist who spent years reporting inside the AI industry, argues in her book *Empire of AI* that the pursuit of **artificial general intelligence** has ceased to be an engineering project and become something closer to a religious vocation. The people building it, she found, are not merely optimistic or worried — they are believers. The object of belief is a machine that may not yet exist, but whose coming feels, to many in the field, as inevitable as prophecy.
