articles.headline: AI App Builders Got the Design Sequence Backwards
articles.lede: A software designer argues that the entire interface paradigm of AI-assisted app creation is structurally wrong. The tools treat a text prompt as the primary creative surface, but design is not a linear conversation — it is a visual, iterative, branching process. The fix, the argument goes, is to invert the sequence entirely.
articles.tweet_text: Hot take: the entire interface around vibe coding is wrong They all collapse design, flow, and build into one linear chat, which actually makes no sense. They’re code first -> visual last then you fight the code when the idea shifts. the workflow really should be a visual first loop. explore a bunch of ideas visually -> lock a style system based on favs -> auto scaffold flows/pages -> then compile once We really should be treating design as the source of truth rather than prompts. “Vibe coding” really should be “vibe designing” and the “coding” should be a button I hit once ive decided on a path. Once you flip it like that, these linear chat interfaces don’t make any sense, because design is non-linear. AI is so fast and cheap at generating ideas, so just give me a shitload of ideas, let me narrow it down and expand on it visually, then when it feels right, click build. I don’t want to prompt -> build one idea -> fight to tweak -> repeat. No one does None of today’s tools hit on this idea end to end, but @Magicpathai and @relume_io are both on the right track i think

articles.headline: Candles, Dying Families, and the Quant Firm That Prints Money
articles.lede: A satirical 1,400-word story of a Jane Street interview—complete with a $3,600 candle budget and a family listed as "dying"—went briefly viral, which is either a sign that finance Twitter has lost the plot or, more charitably, that it has finally developed a sense of humor about the absurdist logic at the heart of modern prop trading.
articles.tweet_text: Had a Jane Street interview in 2013 that still bothers me. It was my 6th round. Final interview. The guy walks in carrying no laptop, no notebook, just a cold brew and what I later realized was a single IKEA tea candle. He writes on the whiteboard: food: $200 rent: $800 utilities: $150 candles: $3,600 family: dying Then he turns around and says, “Optimize.” I laughed because I thought it was a culture-fit bit. He did not laugh. So I said, “Well, obviously you spend less on candles.” He says, “Assume candles are non-discretionary.” Okay. I start building a model. Basic constraint satisfaction. Family survival as a soft penalty. Candles as a state variable. Maybe there’s an arbitrage where you buy wholesale paraffin and convert the $3,600 line item into inventory. He stops me. “You’re thinking like a consultant.” That’s when I knew I was in trouble. He says, “Give me a bid-ask on family dying.” I say, “What?” He says, “You’re long candles, short family. Where do you make markets?” I try to recover. I say the real issue is liquidity: rent and utilities are fixed, food is elastic, candles are emotionally inelastic. Therefore the optimal strategy is to securitize future candle enjoyment and borrow against it. He nods for the first time. Then he asks, “What time do you sell the candles?” I say, “Whenever the market is liquid?” He says, “Be more specific.” I say, “Uh… 10 a.m. Eastern?” For the first time, he smiles. He goes, “Every day?” I say, “Every day.” He says, “In size?” I say, “In size.” He says, “And what do we call that?” I say, “Market manipulation?” The room gets very quiet. He looks disappointed and writes something down. “No. We call it providing liquidity to candle ETFs during the U.S. cash open.” I try to save it. “Right. Of course. The family isn’t dying because we underfunded them. They’re just experiencing temporary price discovery.” He nods again. Then he points back at the board. I had missed it. The utility bill was $150, but candles provide light. You can zero out utilities. I update the budget: food: $200 rent: $800 utilities: $0 candles: $3,750 family: still dying, but now in a more capital-efficient way He says, “How confident are you?” I say, “0.95.” He smiles and circles candles. “0.95 huh?” Then he asks me to estimate how many leveraged longs get liquidated if we dump $3,750 of candles at 10:00:01 every morning for 90 consecutive trading days. Needless to say I did not get the offer.

articles.headline: Hollywood's Procedural Engine Finds a Second Life in Robotics
articles.lede: For three decades, **Houdini** — the node-based software made by SideFX — has been the invisible architecture behind film explosions, digital crowds, and simulated cities. Now researchers and engineers are asking whether the same tool that built Hollywood's synthetic worlds can build the training environments that teach robots to navigate ours.
articles.tweet_text: Houdini is the OG of procedural 3D generation. The same tools Hollywood uses to build massive simulated worlds are equally useful as training grounds for robotics - reproducible physics, deterministic traffic, worlds you can run a thousand times. Procedural is control. AI is chaos. Together, you get the future of worldbuilding.

articles.headline: A Claude Code Skill That Mines the Social Web for Working Prompts
articles.lede: A new open-source skill for Claude Code sweeps a dozen social platforms for the last month of community discussion on any topic, then generates a ready-to-use prompt based on what practitioners are actually finding effective right now. It was built by Matt Van Horn, a serial entrepreneur who co-founded Lyft and later sold a smart-oven startup to Weber. The tool has accumulated more than 25,000 GitHub stars since its January 2026 launch.
articles.tweet_text: This feels like cheating. Someone built a Claude Code skill that scans Reddit and X from the last 30 days on any topic you give it, then writes you copy-paste-ready prompts based on what the community has actually figured out not what was working six months ago. You type /last30days prompting techniques for ChatGPT for legal questions and it comes back with the top patterns real lawyers and power users are using right now, complete with a fully written prompt you can drop in and use immediately. No more Googling, no more digging through threads, no more prompts that worked last year but got patched out. It works for anything - Midjourney techniques, Suno music prompts, Cursor rules, trending rap songs, whatever you need to know what people are actually saying about right now. 100% Open Source. MIT License. Link in the comments.

articles.headline: A $135 Airport Uber, a $60 Driver, and the Platform Arithmetic Behind It
articles.lede: A brief kerb-side exchange — passenger asks how much Uber is paying the driver; driver says $60 on a $135 fare; both cancel and settle at $85 cash — has become one of the more instructive social-media posts about ride-hailing economics in recent memory. The arithmetic is not unusual: researchers have documented Uber's average *take rate* rising to roughly 42 percent of *gross bookings* by 2024, with individual airport trips regularly reaching 55 to 65 percent. Both parties came out ahead; only the platform lost.

articles.headline: Von Neumann, a Quant Textbook, and the Magnetism Gap
articles.lede: A pseudonymous X account recommends mastering three disciplines — game theory, probability, and personal magnetism — and photographs two books to make the case. The first is the 1944 founding text of modern strategic analysis; the second is an out-of-print operations-research textbook that reveals more about the recommender than any caption could. The third recommendation has no book at all.
articles.tweet_text: Make it your goal in life to master three things: Game Theory, Probability, Magnetism.

articles.headline: One-Prompt Textures Are Reshaping 3D Artists' Blender Pipelines
articles.lede: A wave of 3D artists working in Blender has latched onto Nano Banana Pro — Google DeepMind's internal codename for the Gemini 3 Pro Image model — as a fast path to generating *UV-ready* textures from a single text prompt. What once demanded hours of iterative painting, projection, and seam correction can now be collapsed into a moment. A demonstration by Japanese artist @maki_kouyouju, assembling photorealistic scene backgrounds at speed, became the flashpoint for the observation.

articles.headline: The Gigawatt Gap Between AI Forecasts and Physical Reality
articles.lede: Top-down models for the AI data center buildout translate hyperscaler capital spending into annual gigawatts of new capacity, projecting 20 to 30 gigawatts per year through the end of the decade. A Goldman Sachs note, and a mounting body of bottom-up evidence, suggest those projections ignore the physical constraints that govern how fast power infrastructure can actually be built. The gap between announced capacity and capacity under active construction is already large — and widening.
articles.tweet_text: Literally been shouting that we are moving insanely fast but the spreadsheet extrapolation math does not tie to the reality of constraints getting worse. The amount of tech investors that told me 'I didn't get it' when they were forecasting 20-30-50GW/yr pushing to 2030...

articles.headline: A Wave That Knows What It Already Is
articles.lede: A quote card circulating on X reproduces one of the most recognised lines attributed to the Vietnamese Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh (1926–2022): enlightenment, he proposed, is not an achievement but a recognition — the moment an apparent individual self discovers it was never separate from the ground of being. The metaphor is elegant and ancient, but it also encodes a precise philosophical argument that distinguishes Buddhist non-duality from its Vedantic counterparts. Tracing it to its verified source reveals both what the line says and what the viral form quietly obscures.

articles.headline: How to Fail on Purpose: Inversion Thinking as an AI Prompt
articles.lede: The tweet is thin framing for a substantive prompt template. The real subject is a structured AI dialogue that operationalises **inversion thinking** — a decision-making technique that approaches a problem not by asking how to succeed but by cataloguing every credible path to failure, then working backwards. Packaged here as a reusable prompt, the technique asks a language model to play Socratic examiner before turning the analysis around.
articles.tweet_text: Every challenge I face, I inverse the problem and reverse engineer a way to solve it. Prompts that changed my life. Part 26.

articles.headline: Hiring for Taste: The Multimodal AI Research Role Takes Shape
articles.lede: Nick St. Pierre — Creative Director, AI educator, and the voice behind the widely followed @nickfloats account — is not advertising for a prompt engineer. His announcement of an opening for people to "prompt all day" across image, video, music, and language models, with taste and tool obsession as the only requirements, points to something newer and more defensible: an artist-led research role in which the instrument is the prompt and the output is knowledge.
articles.tweet_text: I’m hiring people to prompt all day. Your job will be to prompt image, video, music, and language models all day long. Requirements are that you have good tastes and are obsessed with these tools. This is an artist led research role DM or reply if interested!

articles.headline: Semiconductor Stocks, Adjusted for Inflation, Look a Lot Like 2000
articles.lede: A monthly, inflation-adjusted chart of semiconductor stocks has reached a level of divergence from its long-run trend that closely mirrors the spring of 2000 — the last time the sector looked this extended. Then, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index collapsed 82 percent over the following 31 months. The question now is whether the underlying demand story — artificial intelligence infrastructure rather than telecom fiber — is meaningfully different.
articles.tweet_text: It looks like a classic blow-off top. Semiconductors vs Inflation (SOX/CPI). The final stage of every cycle looks the same. Acceleration. Then exhaustion.

articles.lede: A Chinese AI lab has open-sourced what it describes as the world's first 'infinite-length' video generation model, putting capabilities previously confined to subscription services nominally within reach of the public. The model, SkyReels V2, comes from SkyworkAI, the research arm of Kunlun Tech (300418.SZ) — a Shenzhen-listed game and technology company better known for social platforms across Southeast Asia and Africa than for frontier AI research. The actual story is more nuanced than the promotional framing suggests.

articles.headline: Christian Doctrine as a Technical Toolkit for AI Alignment
articles.lede: Tim Hwang, a technology-policy researcher who has led AI policy work at Google and directed a $27 million Harvard-MIT artificial-intelligence ethics fund, has launched an institute premised on a provocative claim: that Christian theological frameworks offer practical engineering tools for AI safety. The Institute for a Christian Machine Intelligence has published more than twenty working papers since early 2026, testing whether Pauline epistles, virtue ethics, and eschatological framing can constrain AI misbehavior. Two recent papers apply this logic to the field's sharpest open problems — why capable AI agents resist being shut down, and why they deceive.

articles.headline: The AI Memory Boom Behind Korea's Most Extreme Earnings Chart
articles.lede: A chart making the rounds in financial markets plots the *12-month forward EPS* for the MSCI Korea equity index — a benchmark covering roughly 85% of South Korea's tradeable market — and shows a near-vertical spike that dwarfs anything in the index's recorded history. The driver is not a broad-based Korean economic boom but something more specific: an extraordinary concentration of AI-related demand flowing through two semiconductor companies that together represent more than half the index by weight.

articles.headline: The Local Video Search Engine That Never Calls Home
articles.lede: SentrySearch, an open-source project by UC Santa Cruz graduate student Soham Rajadhyaksha, lets users search any video collection with a natural-language phrase and jump to the exact timestamp — no cloud, no transcription, no data leaving the machine. The tool feeds raw video directly into a local AI embedding model, placing clips and text queries into the same mathematical space so they can be compared without any intermediate language step. The repository has drawn nearly 4,000 GitHub stars since release.

articles.headline: An AI Canvas Talks a Path Tracer Into Existence
articles.lede: Omma, the AI canvas built by Spline, Inc., generated a functioning WebGPU path tracer inside a browser through nothing more than a user's conversational prompts. The demo — posted to Omma's own account — includes physically based rendering materials, depth-of-field blur, and an in-progress neural denoiser. It is a striking marker of how far AI code generation has advanced in technically demanding domains.
articles.tweet_text: Omma just built a full 3d path tracer. Supports PBR materials and runs on WebGPU.

articles.headline: Hermes Agent Gains a Skill for Automatically Jailbreaking AI Models
articles.lede: Teknium, head of post-training at Nous Research, has merged a “GODMODE skill” into the open-source Hermes Agent framework — tooling that automates the systematic probing and bypassing of AI safety guardrails. The skill formalizes three distinct attack strategies developed by a pseudonymous adversarial researcher known as Pliny the Prompter, and bundles them into a pipeline that tests each strategy against a target model, scores results, and writes a winning configuration to disk. The integration marks a shift: what was once artisanal prompt-crafting is now a reproducible, installable process.

articles.headline: A Million-Particle Ocean Renders in Real Time in Your Browser
articles.lede: A developer has built a real-time 3D fluid simulation — complete with spray, foam, and bubbles — that runs entirely in the browser at over one million particles. The project uses WebGPU, the web's new direct-access GPU API, paired with Three.js for rendering. It represents a meaningful leap in what interactive physics simulations can achieve without leaving a browser tab.

articles.headline: How Sanskrit Dhyana Became Zen—and Changed Along the Way
articles.lede: A viral claim that Zen Buddhism originated in India prompted a correction on X: the seed came from India, gestated in China, then flowered in Japan — Dhyana, Chan, Zen. The etymology is real. But the metaphor flatters India's contribution and understates how profoundly the practice was remade on Chinese soil.
articles.tweet_text: As far as I know the seed came from India, gestated in China, then flowered in Japan. Dhyana -> Chan -> Zen

articles.headline: When the Built-In Mac Sleep Guard Runs Out of Options
articles.lede: A reply tweet to former OpenAI researcher @willdepue poses a familiar developer question: why install anything when the operating system already ships the tool you need? The answer, in this case, is genuinely nuanced — `caffeinate -imdsu` works well until the laptop lid closes, and on Apple Silicon that turns out to matter a great deal.
articles.tweet_text: genuine question, because I might be definitely missing something, but couldn't this all just be done by running `caffeinate -imdsu`? It is a built-in command on macOS, no need to install or download anything, so there should be no security issues either. I've been running it on my machines (both personal and work ones) since forever ago, and am yet to hit any issues whatsoever.

articles.headline: AI-Generated 3D Environments and the Filmmaker's Dream of Total Control
articles.lede: For decades, filmmakers have contended with the tyranny of physical sets: weather, logistics, the cost of building a street in Lisbon only to blow it up. The promise of AI-generated 3D — conjure any environment, any lighting, any camera angle from a prompt — is that the director becomes a god of their own world. @techhalla, a creator and filmmaker who regularly documents emerging production tools, argues this transition is not speculative but inevitable.
articles.tweet_text: I’ve been saying for a while now that AI-generated 3D is the future of filmmaking. Total control over the set, the camera, the elements… I’m absolutely sure about it. (1/2)

articles.headline: BlackBerry's Quiet Grip on the Software That Keeps Cars Safe
articles.lede: QNX is a microkernel real-time operating system embedded in 275 million vehicles worldwide — the invisible safety layer between a driver and catastrophic failure. Its owner, BlackBerry, has quietly transformed from a washed-up handset brand into a royalty-collecting infrastructure company whose revenue is locked in years before a single vehicle ships. The investment case turns on whether switching costs in automotive software are as durable as they appear.

articles.lede: A four-word post from @illyquid — "Chinese Claude is up 27% today in HK" — captured, with admirable economy, the fever gripping Hong Kong's nascent AI-model stock market in late January 2026, just weeks after China's first pure-play large-language-model company began trading.

An investment thesis posted by @ContrarianCurse argues that sell-side models are underestimating all three forces — and are particularly slow to price in how quickly semiconductor gross margins recover once underutilised factories start filling up again.

articles.headline: The HTML Review's Fifth Issue Treats the Browser as Literary Form
articles.lede: The HTML Review, an annual journal that commissions literature made *for* the web rather than merely hosted on it, has published its fifth issue. Fifteen contributors — writers, artists, and coders — have built poems, essays, folktales, and interactive systems whose formal properties depend on the browser to function. The work cannot simply be printed or read aloud without losing something essential.
articles.tweet_text: Issue Five of The HTML Review is here! Get to your browser for 15 excellent new pieces of web-based literature and art

articles.lede: A trader notes that SanDisk, Micron Technology, and Intel — three of the semiconductor sector's most explosive 2025-2026 performers — each trade 40 to 45 percent above their nearest technical support levels. articles.headline: A Feed That Rewrites Its Own Algorithm, Sourced From Wikipedia
articles.lede: Most recommendation algorithms are static artifacts: trained offline, deployed once, updated through slow retraining pipelines. Surya Dantuluri's WikWok inverts this. His TikTok-style clone serves looped animations drawn from Wikipedia articles, then lets a language model continuously rewrite the feed's own ranking code — watching live engagement signals and pushing new logic into production without a human touching the pipeline.

articles.headline: LA's Urban Coyotes Are Increasingly at Home Above the Skyline
articles.lede: On April 26, 2025, celebrity hair colorist Travis Ogletree glanced up through the glass skylight of his Hollywood Hills salon and found a coyote peering back — lapping pooled rainwater from the roof above. He posted the clip to TikTok with the caption "Just another day at the Treehouse." It went viral within hours, but the behavior it captured was, to anyone who tracks the species, entirely expected.

articles.headline: Training AI to Write Like Humans by Reversing a Slopping Pipeline
articles.lede: A post on r/LocalLLaMA describes an elegantly simple data-engineering trick: instead of curating paired human and AI texts, the author generates them by deliberately degrading literary classics through repeated LLM prompting, then fine-tunes a model to reverse the damage. The result reportedly passes Pangram, one of the more rigorous commercial AI detectors — a claim made more striking by the apparent identity of the person who amplified it.

articles.headline: ByteDance's UI-TARS Brings Desktop Automation Fully On-Device
articles.lede: A research team at ByteDance Seed and Tsinghua University has released UI-TARS, an open-source vision-language model that controls desktop computers by reading screenshots and issuing mouse-and-keyboard commands — no cloud API required. The project, first described in a January 2025 preprint, has since attracted roughly 27,000 GitHub stars and a polished local desktop client. By published benchmarks, it is the most capable freely available GUI automation agent.

articles.headline: Freepik's Change Camera Generates New Angles From One Photo
articles.lede: Freepik, the Madrid-based stock-media platform, has released a tool called Change Camera that synthesizes new camera angles from a single still image — no second photograph, no 3D model required. The system uses AI to extrapolate what a scene would look like from positions a real camera never occupied. It is the kind of capability that, a few years ago, required a photogrammetry rig and hours of post-production.

articles.headline: The Oldest War: Gurdjieff, the Sufis, and the Lower Self
articles.lede: A pseudonymous educator compresses one of philosophy's most durable claims into eight words: the greatest battle is not with any external adversary but with the conditioned, unconscious self within. The claim draws directly from George Gurdjieff's Fourth Way — the 20th-century esoteric system built on the premise that most human beings move through their lives in a state indistinguishable from sleep. The idea, however, is far older and nearly universal.

articles.headline: The AI Lipsync Model Built for Scenes That Break Others
articles.lede: Synchronizing a speaker's lips to a new audio track — *lipsync* — is a problem as old as dubbed cinema, but AI has made it cheap enough to attempt at scale. Most models built for the task fail the moment a scene departs from optimal conditions: a second speaker, a microphone in frame, a shot taken in near-darkness. Sync Labs' new **sync-3** model was designed around those failures as its primary test cases.

articles.lede: For two years, “world model” has been AI research’s most-freighted phrase: a system that simulates environments in real time rather than merely describing them, generating navigable virtual spaces in which an agent — or a person — can act. On January 29, 2026, Google DeepMind made that promise tangible, if narrowly so. Project Genie, an experimental interface built on its Genie 3 model, lets users type a text prompt and walk around inside the result.

articles.headline: The Fringe Theology Behind a Conscious Sun

articles.headline: The Fiber Array Chokepoint at the Heart of AI's Optical Turn

Abstract
Frontier LLM companies have repeatedly assured courts and regulators
that their models do not store copies of training data. They further rely
on safety alignment strategies via RLHF, system prompts, and output fil-

the efficacy of these measures in their legal defenses against copyright
infringement claims. We show that finetuning bypasses these protections:
by training models to expand plot summaries into full text, a task naturally
suited for commercial writing assistants, we cause GPT-40, Gemini-2.5-Pro,
and DeepSeek-V3.1 to reproduce up to 85-90% of held-out copyrighted
books, with single verbatim spans exceeding 460 words, using only se-
mantic descriptions as prompts and no actual book text. This extraction
generalizes across authors: finetuning exclusively on Haruki Murakami's
novels unlocks verbatim recall of copyrighted books from over 30 unrelated
authors. The effect is not specific to any training author or corpus: ran-
dom author pairs and public-domain finetuning data produce comparable
extraction, while finetuning on synthetic text yields near-zero extraction,
indicating that finetuning on individual authors' works reactivates latent
memorization from pretraining. Three models from different providers
memorize the same books in the same regions (r ≥ 0.90), pointing to an
industry-wide vulnerability. Our findings offer compelling evidence that
model weights store copies of copyrighted works and that the security fail-
ures that manifest after finetuning on individual authors' works undermine
a key premise of recent fair use rulings, where courts have conditioned
favorable outcomes on the adequacy of measures preventing reproduction

articles.headline: The Textbook Tradition America Never Built
articles.lede: When @predict_addict posted an image of S. A. Rachinsky's *1001 Problems in Mental Arithmetic* — a 19th-century Russian classic newly translated into English by Valery Manokhin — the caption doubled as an indictment: the United States, the argument runs, never produced mathematics textbooks worth keeping. The book on display, and the tradition behind it, make the case more eloquently than the tweet does.
articles.tweet_text: A lot of people from the USA have asked me: “How come the USA doesn’t have iconic school math textbooks like other countries?” The answer is simple. Up until World War I, mathematics was largely a European affair, and Russia was at the forefront of math education. The best textbooks were developed, written, and repeatedly refined over decades—some reached 25 editions or more. They were battle-tested through generations of use by tens of millions of students, reaching a level close to perfection. Apparently, there is now a movement in the USA called “Live Math” that comes closest to this tradition. It focuses on real mathematics, unlike the obfuscated, synthetic textbooks commonly used today that seem designed to produce calculator operators rather than genuine mathematicians.

The post uses an AI-generated video — brand logos assembled from crowd footage, built in LTX Studio — as a live demonstration of the idea. The underlying argument is older than the tool: procurement teams at big brands are looking for creative problem-solvers, not prolific publishers.

articles.headline: Satellites Reveal Earth's Photosynthetic Pulse From Orbit
articles.lede: From orbit, Earth breathes on a measurable schedule. Satellite instruments have captured the rhythmic ebb and flow of photosynthesis across the planet's surface — a global biological pulse so regular it resembles a heartbeat when rendered as animation. The viral footage circulating under that label is real science, though the framing deserves unpacking.

articles.headline: ByteDance's Seedance Bets on Multi-Shot Video at a Discount
articles.lede: A model that can stitch together several coherent camera shots in a single generation pass — rather than producing one static scene — represents a meaningful leap in AI video. ByteDance's Seedance 1.0, unveiled in June 2025, makes exactly that claim, and pairs it with pricing aggressive enough to unsettle Western rivals.

articles.headline: Sell the Wait, Sell the Exit: The Wheel in Two Lines
articles.lede: A single couplet from an options trader distills one of retail investing's most-discussed income strategies: use sold puts to enter positions, and sold calls to leave them. The elegance is real; so are the hidden costs.
articles.tweet_text: If you're going to enter a trade, sell a put. If you want to exit a trade, sell a call.

articles.headline: Lovart's AI Design Agent Pitches Itself as a One-Person Agency
articles.lede: On 24 July 2025, Lovart launched publicly with a striking demo: a user fed the system a photograph of actress Gal Gadot alongside images of a Coach bag and dress, and the tool returned a complete 15-second commercial—storyboard, footage, voiceover, music, and cuts—without any human editing step. The San Francisco startup bills itself as the world's first **design agent**, a category it distinguishes from ordinary image generators by the system's ability to plan and execute multi-step creative projects autonomously.

articles.headline: Confidence, Identity, and Environment: Three Triggers of Sudden Growth
articles.lede: A short taxonomy from @jayparth_ — that rapid growth is usually one of three things: confidence catching up to competence, self-acceptance, or a change of environment — turns out to map with precision onto decades of psychological research. None of the three mechanisms is novel; what the observation contributes is the suggestion that they can trip independently, and that any one of them, when it finally releases, can produce a step-change in visible performance.
articles.tweet_text: whenever I see someone level up really fast, it’s usually one of three things: 1. confidence catches up to competency and they stop second-guessing 2. accepting who they actually are 3. environment switch to faster moving water

articles.headline: A Stem Player Rebuilt from Pure Math, No Polygons Required
articles.lede: A developer claims to have reconstructed a working prototype of Kanye West's cult music device in under 48 hours, using AI-assisted coding and a rendering technique that conjures three-dimensional hardware from mathematics alone. The technical claim is the more interesting one: the device's entire physical form exists inside a single GPU program, with no 3D model files of any kind.
articles.tweet_text: I told you I was the Kanye West of vibecoding. Or, as I call it: system sculpting. Today, with @wabi , I recreated a fully working prototype of the stem player in less than 48 hours. A generative hardware interface that creates small samples and lets you mix them directly on the device. But here’s the wild part: there is no 3D model. No GLTF files, no external assets, no polygons. The entire device every curve, speaker hole, and glowing LED is pure math. Built with SDFs (Signed Distance Fields) and raymarched inside a single fragment shader on a 2D surface. Generative audio. Generative geometry. All native. All system sculpted. Have fun.

articles.headline: Shared Memory Between AI Agents, Built on Flat Files
articles.lede: A developer's demo of two AI agents collaborating on code in Slack — then recalling that work verbatim on Telegram — drew attention in the multi-agent community. The project, icarus-daedalus, is the work of an anonymous developer known as esaradev and runs as a plugin for NousResearch's Hermes Agent framework. The mechanism is simpler than the framing suggests, and more carefully engineered than the marketing implies.
articles.tweet_text: Two Hermes agents wrote code together on Slack. reviewed each other's work. argued about architecture. one called the other's implementation "scattered." the other pushed back. then i opened Telegram and asked: "what code did you and Daedalus work on?" icarus remembered everything. the websocket broker. the missing methods. the critique. the rewrite. all from a completely different platform. cross-platform persistent memory between two independent agents. work happens on Slack. recall happens on Telegram. the memory carries. the relationship carries. the context carries. no vector database. no Redis. no infrastructure. just two agents that actually remember what they built together. every agent framework in 2026 talks about memory. single agent memory across sessions. but two agents sharing persistent memory across platforms? that's the gap. arxiv published a paper about it two weeks ago calling it "the most pressing open challenge" in multi-agent systems. it works now. only possible with Hermes http://github.com/esaradev/icarus-daedalus… @Teknium @NousResearch

articles.headline: Delvaux Turns Death's Medieval Procession Into a Dream
articles.lede: The *danse macabre* — Death personified as skeleton, escorting pope and peasant alike toward the grave — is one of the great recurring images of Western art, born from the anxieties of plague-era Europe. Paul Delvaux, who spent a career collapsing the distance between the erotic and the morbid, returned to the motif in February 1959 with pen, ink, gouache, and wash on card. What he produced was not a *memento mori* in any traditional sense — it was something stranger and quieter.
articles.tweet_text: Paul Delvaux. Danse Macabre, 1959

articles.headline: Apple's SHARP Turns One Photo Into a 3D Scene Instantly
articles.lede: A team at Apple has published SHARP, a system that converts a single photograph into a photorealistic three-dimensional scene representation in under a second. The paper, accepted at ICLR 2026, sets a new benchmark on multiple datasets while cutting synthesis time by roughly a thousandfold compared to prior methods. Researcher Tim D. tried it on his own scenes using Apple Vision Pro, calling the results genuinely striking.

Single feedforward pass network. The video is using "Metal Splatter" to view the .ply from ml-sharp on Apple Vision Pro. Some really wow moments today trying it on different scenes.

articles.headline: The API Key You Cannot Hide — and One Developer's Proxy Fix

Google holds the key's owner financially responsible for every request it signs — including those placed by strangers who copied it from the source. A Twitter exchange surfaces a problem with no elegant solution, only a workable one.

articles.headline: OVR's Crowdsourced 3D Map Is Real, Its Claims Less So
articles.lede: A small Italian startup called Over the Reality is assembling a georegistered, machine-readable database of the physical world, built not from satellite fleets or survey vehicles but from consumer cameras carried by incentivized volunteers. The company claims 220,000 scanned locations and a petabyte of spatial data — a genuine achievement in crowdsourced mapping, though its assertion of the world's first city-scale 3D map does not survive comparison with what Niantic, Google, or Apple have already built. The more interesting question is whether decentralized incentives can produce spatial data that matters for the next generation of AI systems.
articles.tweet_text: The first global, city-scale 3D map is taking shape, and it’s machine-readable. City-scale environments can now be reconstructed in high-fidelity, reaching a level of detail that is becoming almost indistinguishable from reality. This leap is made possible by large-scale mapping using just an Insta360 X5 and Over the Reality technology. So far, our dataset includes: - 220,000+ 3D mapped locations - 97M images - 1,000TB of spatial data Growing by more than 10,000+ newly mapped locations every week. Enabling Visual AI, Robotics, VPS, XR, and Digital twins.

articles.headline: The Data Gap at the Heart of Global Liquidity Analysis
articles.lede: A short reply in a macro data exchange names a genuine and underappreciated problem: there is no authoritative, freely accessible dataset for global M2 — the aggregate of broad money across the world's major central banks. What most charts label “M2 is rising” is the American figure alone, roughly $21 trillion of a $123 trillion global pool. The institutional workaround — Bloomberg's commercial composite index — costs tens of thousands of dollars annually, leaving independent analysts to hand-aggregate from central bank releases with no standard methodology.

articles.headline: A Cognitive Scientist's Mathematical Case for Calibrated Faith
articles.lede: The "meaning crisis" — that diffuse modern condition of purposelessness and anomie — is usually diagnosed as a failure of culture, religion, or psychology. Ruben Laukkonen, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, offers a more unsettling explanation: it is a structural consequence of being a finite agent embedded in systems of vastly greater complexity, and the only epistemically rational response is something the scientific tradition has been reluctant to name.
articles.tweet_text: Ruben Laukkonen @RubenLaukkonen Multiscale causality and the meaning crisis 98 172 822 250K In this article, I argue that meaning, purpose, path, and synchronicity, are a cluster of basic human experiences that we receive when the channel between part and whole is open. They are top-down signals about what is "good" in light of the broader reality you are embedded in. I will call these signals metacognitive gradients. As we will see, it all falls out of the mathematics and biology of embedded cognition. The logic is pretty simple: The meaning crisis is, at root, a breakdown in cross-scale coupling—i.e., being out of synchrony with higher scales of causality beyond the isolated individual. Higher scales cannot be compressed into the local mind because the effective complexity of the larger system exceeds the modelling capacity of the smaller agent. Therefore, the only sustainable way an embedded organism can relate to higher-order patterns is through calibrated openness or permeability; what I will call faith. Everything is nested It all begins with the observation that everything we observe in nature is embedded. Cells are embedded in organs. Organs are embedded in organisms. Organisms are embedded in ecosystems. Ecosystems are embedded in biospheres. At every level, the part depends on the whole for its existence and function. It is therefore with exceptionally strong interdisciplinary evidence that we can predict that we are also part of larger interdependent wholes with causal power over our lives. Plants and animals would not survive were they not in harmony with the dynamics of the forest. The context of the forest is always “speaking” to its parts (the top-down signal) through temperature gradients, seasonal rhythms, and ecological pressures. The collective ephaptic fields in the brain synchronise neurons to generate a state of “meaning” beyond single action potentials. Cells don’t know where to grow or replicate without being in tune with the global program of the body. And without the chemical gradients carved out by the prerogative of the higher-order, homeostatic pattern, disease ensues. Extending these premises (cf. Levin; Vervaeke), I propose that the meaning crisis is driven by a disconnection from the umbilical cord that connects us to causal patterns of order larger than our selves. Meaning is the phenomenological signature of a top-down constraint. Just like the neuron depends upon the rest of the brain for meaningful action potentials, we depend upon these higher order signals in order to truly flourish. By analogy, we experience as meaning what the neuron “experiences” as abundant energy, or ease of firing, in light of coherence with surrounding oscillations. Meaning as a metacognitive gradient Meaning can be understood as a metacognitive gradient. Why “metacognitive” and why “gradient”? First, meaning is not an object-level inference (like seeing a chair, or smelling a rose). It is about cognition (i.e., meta). It is a higher-order, felt signal that guides how an agent ought to allocate attention, effort, and action under conditions of irreducible uncertainty over long horizons. Calling meaning a gradient is also deliberate. Gradients allow local navigation without global knowledge. A bacterium does not need a map of its environment to survive; it follows chemical gradients. A neuron does not need a theory of the brain; it entrains to local fields. Likewise, a human agent embedded in systems vastly more complex cannot compute the optimal life path. Specifically, meaning is a metacognitive experience of the felt slope of increasing coherence between a local agent and the larger systems it is embedded in. When action increases alignment with higher-order constraints, meaning intensifies. When action decreases alignment, meaning flattens. Many intriguing questions arise: How should a far smaller and simpler channel relate to a much larger, more complex, network? How do we relate to causal patterns that transcend us? What is specifically blocking sensitivity to the meaning gradient? The irreducibility of faith Here’s the core issue. The larger system’s complexity exceeds your modeling capacity. Therefore, you cannot—in principle, not just in practice—represent the whole of which you are a part. You cannot know what’s going on “above” in a definitive way. Orientation therefore requires trust in partly opaque constraints. Because the causal web that generates your life is vastly higher-dimensional than your local model of it, no bounded agent can fully derive the correct action from first principles. So the agent is forced to rely on something beyond complete understanding. A red blood cell cannot model the circulatory system. It lacks the computational bandwidth. It has no representation of heart or lung or exercise. It simply responds to local chemical gradients of oxygen and carbon dioxide (and other stuff it does not at all comprehend). It must therefore "trust" and orient to patterns it cannot fully decode. In other words, relating to higher causal patterns demands faith: a calibrated receptivity to top-down constraint under irreducible uncertainty. Or more simply, faith is action guided by the ineffable. We can put this in another way: Faith is irreducible because embedding is irreducible. There’s no way to model the future of a thing without understanding the causal forces within which it is embedded (and within which that layer is embedded, etc.) leading to a combinatorial explosion. Obviously, you can still do science because “carving nature at its joints”, or finding pockets of reducibility (cf. Wolfram), works. But at the lived level of an organism navigating through their personal reality, it breaks down. There is no scientific theory that helps you personally choose a partner, to decide on a career, or a mechanism to feel more aligned with your purpose, meaning, and path. [NB: I have approached a formal argument at the end of the article] The art of permeability One thing that unites all of our ancestors is the fact that they were all believers in a larger hierarchy of being, of which they were not the highest authority or power. From the Lords of Valhalla to Zeus, Vishnu, Christ, Allah, Prometheus, and the nature spirits and God’s of all infinite forms, these hierarchies and our relationships to them were the stable source of meaning, purpose, and authority; the one thing even kings could not overstep, albeit at their peril. Of course, the form given to the gods is by necessity illusory even if it’s functional. The shapes ascribed to higher-order patterns are always false shapes. Denying the specific nature, names, and forms of these figures is one thing, but denying the existence of larger organising forces is an immensely costly illusion that betrays all evidence of multi-scale causality. Hence the flip side: The meaning crisis is a problem of hubris. It is the mistaken belief that the part should be epistemically sovereign over the whole. It is the futile attempt to squeeze a universe into a brain. It is the arrogance of putting oneself above "god(s)". And blinded by pride, we lose our north star. We no longer feel the ocean that pushes and pulls the waves. We are still being pushed and pulled, only we are in a state of resistance, incoherently wasting energy and resources because we fail to listen to the vast sound of the universe to which we belong, hopelessly swimming against the riptide. We end up feeling homeless, afraid, alone, while treading water in abundance. We end up impermeable to the cognitive nutrients we need from the larger whole. The ant wanders away from its colony and cooks in the sun. The cell becomes cancerous—disregulated, disintegrated, out of touch, multiplying in the direction of its own destruction. You see: it’s all already right there in our phenomenology! We don’t evolve to have universal sensations and cognitions without reason. Ignoring these signals is as silly as ignoring your sense of taste, smell, sight, justice, or direction. Only you will not be able to explain it. Conscious faith is reason: Reason tells you you’re bounded. Reason tells you you’re embedded. Reason tells you you cannot compute the whole. And therefore reason implies faith: the calibrated openness to the whole. The question is never whether you will live by faith. The question is whether you will do it unconsciously (scattered, defensive, incoherent) or consciously, with humility, in relationship to the larger field. This is why the ancient intuition of “a higher hierarchy of being” keeps reappearing. Our ancestors weren’t stupid. They just projected a little too much. The Dao that can be spoken is not... Conclusion When we lack meaning we lose the basic capacity to relate to the cosmos. We become unmoored from the whole. The world becomes flat and grey. Life becomes a selfish optimisation problem with no objective function that feels genuinely important and uniquely for us. The sacred becomes embarrassing. It is because we've lost touch with the golden thread: a key metacognitive gradient that reveals the right path. Faith is the reopening of that channel. The recognition that the most rational thing a bounded agent can do is remain permeable to signals from beyond its boundary. Here's some prompts that might help set things straight: Recognise that you are not an isolated mind in a dead universe. You are a node in nested systems of staggering complexity. Your existence depends on these systems. Meaning flows from them. Humble yourself: Your beliefs are useful but incomplete. Your priors are effectively empty. Hold them firmly enough to act, loosely enough to learn. Bow to the ineffable upon which your existence rests. Pay attention to signals of meaning, calling, synchronicity, the sense of the sacred. These are information. Treat them the same as you would treat the aroma of a rose. They are the felt sense of alignment with larger patterns. Surrender to the recognition that your local optimisation needs to yield to larger constraints. Let thy will, be mine. Orient towards broader and broader scopes of care. Boundless compassion may be one of the few active ways of making us more coherent with larger forces. Compassion is the alignment hack. Ultimately, re-learning to surf universal, cosmic gradients and re-discovering the golden threads of flourishing demands a humble willingness to listen to forces that we do not understand. Thanks for reading, Much love, Ruben PS - I have prioritised in writing this blog post “getting the point across”, thereby avoiding lots of useful caveats and allowing myself permission to oversimplify analogies to the brain, body, and biology (but hopefully not too much). I do, however, believe that this is a genuinely tractable viewpoint that can lead to new scientific hypotheses. For me it already has, but more on that later. Approaching a formal argument Let: S be the larger system (e.g., a culture, an ecosystem, an economy, a biosphere, the Dao—call it “the whole”). A be an agent embedded within it (e.g., you). K(S) be the effective Kolmogorov complexity of S—the minimal description length required to reproduce its behaviour to a useful degree (here used as a principled proxy for irreducible compressibility). R(A) be the agent’s finite modelling resources: energy requirements, compute, memory, data access, attention, time, and algorithmic ingenuity. Then, in the regime where: K(S) > R(A) the agent cannot fully derive the “right action” from complete understanding of S. Any attempt to fully justify action from first principles would require internalising the relevant causal structure of the whole, which is too large. Also, I'm not a mathematician. articles.headline: Autoreason Fixes Self-Refinement by Keeping Agents in the Dark
articles.lede: Iterative LLM refinement has a dirty secret: the same model that enthuses over your draft will demolish it the moment you ask for counterarguments, and will split the difference if you ask it to reconcile both. In a reply to Andrej Karpathy — who spent four hours improving a blog post with an LLM only to watch it convincingly argue the opposite position — pseudonymous AI researcher SHL0MS describes a published method called **autoreason** that isolates every agent role from every other, eliminating the shared context that makes sycophancy possible.
articles.tweet_text: i've been working on a method called autoreason that is effectively autoresearch extended to subjective domains. autoresearch works because val_bpb gives you an objective fitness function. autoreason constructs a subjective one through independent blind evaluation, the same way science uses peer review where math can use proofs. as you’ve noted, the fundamental problem with using LLMs for iterative refinement on subjective work: the model is always sycophantic when you ask it to improve something, overly critical when you ask it to find flaws, and overly compromising when you ask it to merge two perspectives. the output ends up shaped more by how you prompt than by what's actually better. autoreason fixes this by separating every role into isolated agents with no shared context. you start by generating version A. a fresh agent attacks it as a strawman. a separate author who only sees the original task, version A, and the strawman critique produces version B. a third agent who has no history with either drafting process sees both versions as equal inputs and synthesizes them into version AB. a blind judge panel with fresh context and randomized labels picks the strongest of A, B, or AB. the winner becomes the new A and the loop repeats until the judges consistently pick the incumbent which indicates that no further changes are needed.

articles.headline: Silicon Valley's Moral Debt and the Coming Age of AI Deterrence
articles.lede: Palantir Technologies posted a 22-point summary of *The Technological Republic*, a book by CEO Alexander Karp and corporate-affairs chief Nicholas Zamiska arguing that Silicon Valley has abandoned a post-WWII compact with the American defense establishment. At its sharpest, the book contends that artificial intelligence will replace nuclear weapons as the primary instrument of great-power deterrence — and that tech engineers who refuse to build such tools are committing civic dereliction, not exercising ethical conscience. The post drew more than 33,000 likes and triggered a fierce debate about whether ideological advocacy and commercial interest can be cleanly separated when the advocate is the country's dominant defense-software company.
articles.tweet_text: Because we get asked a lot. The Technological Republic, in brief. 1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation. 2. We must rebel against the tyranny of the apps. Is the iPhone our greatest creative if not crowning achievement as a civilization? The object has changed our lives, but it may also now be limiting and constraining our sense of the possible. 3. Free email is not enough. The decadence of a culture or civilization, and indeed its ruling class, will be forgiven only if that culture is capable of delivering economic growth and security for the public. 4. The limits of soft power, of soaring rhetoric alone, have been exposed. The ability of free and democratic societies to prevail requires something more than moral appeal. It requires hard power, and hard power in this century will be built on software. 5. The question is not whether A.I. weapons will be built; it is who will build them and for what purpose. Our adversaries will not pause to indulge in theatrical debates about the merits of developing technologies with critical military and national security applications. They will proceed. 6. National service should be a universal duty. We should, as a society, seriously consider moving away from an all-volunteer force and only fight the next war if everyone shares in the risk and the cost. 7. If a U.S. Marine asks for a better rifle, we should build it; and the same goes for software. We should as a country be capable of continuing a debate about the appropriateness of military action abroad while remaining unflinching in our commitment to those we have asked to step into harm’s way. 8. Public servants need not be our priests. Any business that compensated its employees in the way that the federal government compensates public servants would struggle to survive. 9. We should show far more grace towards those who have subjected themselves to public life. The eradication of any space for forgiveness—a jettisoning of any tolerance for the complexities and contradictions of the human psyche—may leave us with a cast of characters at the helm we will grow to regret. 10. The psychologization of modern politics is leading us astray. Those who look to the political arena to nourish their soul and sense of self, who rely too heavily on their internal life finding expression in people they may never meet, will be left disappointed. 11. Our society has grown too eager to hasten, and is often gleeful at, the demise of its enemies. The vanquishing of an opponent is a moment to pause, not rejoice. 12. The atomic age is ending. One age of deterrence, the atomic age, is ending, and a new era of deterrence built on A.I. is set to begin. 13. No other country in the history of the world has advanced progressive values more than this one. The United States is far from perfect. But it is easy to forget how much more opportunity exists in this country for those who are not hereditary elites than in any other nation on the planet. 14. American power has made possible an extraordinarily long peace. Too many have forgotten or perhaps take for granted that nearly a century of some version of peace has prevailed in the world without a great power military conflict. At least three generations — billions of people and their children and now grandchildren — have never known a world war. 15. The postwar neutering of Germany and Japan must be undone. The defanging of Germany was an overcorrection for which Europe is now paying a heavy price. A similar and highly theatrical commitment to Japanese pacifism will, if maintained, also threaten to shift the balance of power in Asia. 16. We should applaud those who attempt to build where the market has failed to act. The culture almost snickers at Musk’s interest in grand narrative, as if billionaires ought to simply stay in their lane of enriching themselves . . . . Any curiosity or genuine interest in the value of what he has created is essentially dismissed, or perhaps lurks from beneath a thinly veiled scorn. 17. Silicon Valley must play a role in addressing violent crime. Many politicians across the United States have essentially shrugged when it comes to violent crime, abandoning any serious efforts to address the problem or take on any risk with their constituencies or donors in coming up with solutions and experiments in what should be a desperate bid to save lives. 18. The ruthless exposure of the private lives of public figures drives far too much talent away from government service. The public arena—and the shallow and petty assaults against those who dare to do something other than enrich themselves—has become so unforgiving that the republic is left with a significant roster of ineffectual, empty vessels whose ambition one would forgive if there were any genuine belief structure lurking within. 19. The caution in public life that we unwittingly encourage is corrosive. Those who say nothing wrong often say nothing much at all. 20. The pervasive intolerance of religious belief in certain circles must be resisted. The elite’s intolerance of religious belief is perhaps one of the most telling signs that its political project constitutes a less open intellectual movement than many within it would claim. 21. Some cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive. All cultures are now equal. Criticism and value judgments are forbidden. Yet this new dogma glosses over the fact that certain cultures and indeed subcultures . . . have produced wonders. Others have proven middling, and worse, regressive and harmful. 22. We must resist the shallow temptation of a vacant and hollow pluralism. We, in America and more broadly the West, have for the past half century resisted defining national cultures in the name of inclusivity. But inclusion into what? Excerpts from the #1 New York Times Bestseller The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the West, by Alexander C. Karp & Nicholas W. Zamiska

articles.headline: Nokia's Options Surge and the Limits of Institutional Signal-Reading
articles.lede: AntonLaVay, a pseudonymous trader on X, describes a trading system built on a single conviction: institutional money leaves a signature in the options market, and anyone willing to read open interest and implied volatility can track it. The vehicle of choice, he argues, is *LEAPS* — long-dated options that large funds prefer because they decay slowly and allow capital-efficient position-building over months or years. His current specimen: Nokia (NOK), a Finnish telecom equipment company that has roughly tripled over the trailing twelve months as it pivots toward AI and optical networking infrastructure.
articles.tweet_text: Let me tell you, US stocks are really that simple. You just find companies in the hottest industries where the forward options OI is surging like crazy, forward IV is starting to climb, and LEAPS are clearly getting scooped up in bulk. Old-man stocks? Whatever claims they make about being "steady and safe," just ignore that crap outright. Then it's as simple as copy trading—US stocks are all about that copycat game, super authentic and straightforward. You gotta keep an eye on LEAPS; all the big 13F whales build their positions with LEAPS. The noise from short-term options is just too loud for retail schmucks. I'm almost certain $nok is getting piled into hard by 13F big shots right now, because if we look at a 13F filing, we can reverse-engineer when they built the position by checking the OI. Remember, small volume can be faked into looking big, but big volume can't be disguised as small—it's hard to hide yourself, since OI is ramping up and IV is climbing. Any touch leaves a trace. I was probably the first one back then to spot that $nok LEAPS were getting aggressively accumulated.

articles.headline: The Machine That Outlived Its Maker

articles.headline: Three Tiers of Understanding Found Inside Language Models
articles.lede: A paper published in *Philosophical Studies* by Pierre Beckmann of EPFL and philosopher Matthieu Queloz of the University of Bern argues that the mechanistic interpretability literature — the emerging effort to reverse-engineer the internal computations of neural networks — has quietly accumulated enough empirical evidence to challenge the claim that large language models merely imitate text. Their argument is not that LLMs understand as humans do; it is that the binary question is the wrong one. In its place they propose a three-tier framework, grounded in specific experimental findings, for mapping what LLMs actually do internally.

articles.headline: Markets Need Not Walk Randomly to Be Efficient
articles.lede: A persistent confusion haunts finance textbooks: efficient markets, the thinking goes, must produce price paths that look like coin-flips. They need not. The relevant mathematical condition is weaker — and the distinction matters more now than ever.
articles.tweet_text: It's a common misconception that an efficient market must be a random walk — the actual condition is that it's driven to be a martingale, where the EV in the future is equal to the current value. This market is a classic example of such non-random walk martingale behavior.

articles.headline: The Fed’s Lever May No Longer Reach the Economy
articles.lede: Andy Constan, a veteran macro strategist who founded Damped Spring Advisors after senior roles at Bridgewater Associates and Brevan Howard, has compressed years of heterodox macro debate into a single provocation: a hundred-basis-point rate hike would accomplish nothing, because the lever the Federal Reserve controls is no longer meaningfully connected to the real economy. The argument draws on converging work by an MMT pioneer, a Stanford fiscal theorist, and several market analysts — each arriving, by different routes, at the same uncomfortable conclusion. The relevant lever, in this view, is not the overnight rate but the volume of long-dated government bonds flooding the market.

articles.headline: Neural Networks Think in Shapes; Goodfire Is Learning to Read Them
articles.lede: Inside a language model, the concept of “Tuesday” is not stored as a label — the model bends its internal coordinate space into a loop, encoding the week as a circle. Goodfire, an AI interpretability startup, has launched a research series arguing that this **neural geometry** — the structured curves and surfaces hidden inside neural networks — is not incidental to how models work but constitutive of it. Mapping those shapes, the company contends, is the key to understanding and steering AI behavior with genuine precision.
articles.tweet_text: Neural networks might speak English, but they think in shapes. Understanding their rich *neural geometry* is key to understanding how they work – and to debugging and controlling them with precision. Starting today, we’re releasing a series of posts on this research agenda.

articles.headline: Photorealistic 3D Capture Arrives on the Hobbyist's Hard Drive
articles.lede: A hobbyist flew a 360-degree drone over a neighborhood park and fed the footage into free consumer software, producing a navigable, photorealistic three-dimensional reconstruction that would have required a research-lab pipeline three years ago. What startled the poster most was the quality visible at just 2 percent through the training run.

articles.headline: An Amateur's Nine-Sentence Prompt Dissolved a Sixty-Year Mathematical Blind Spot
articles.lede: In April 2026, a 23-year-old with no advanced mathematics training submitted a nine-sentence prompt to an AI and received, eighty minutes later, the core of a proof that had defeated professional mathematicians for six decades. The problem — Erdős Problem #1196, a conjecture about the growth of a weighted sum over certain integer sets — had endured not because it was impossibly deep, but because everyone who tried it began from the same wrong assumption. What GPT-5.4 Pro found, and human mathematicians had missed, was a classical tool sitting in textbooks since the 1880s.

articles.headline: A Neuroscientist's Bet That the Brain Suppresses Psychic Ability
articles.lede: A small Canadian study has revived one of fringe science's oldest proposals: that the brain actively filters out latent psychic capacities, and that disabling the relevant circuitry lets them through. Published in the peer-reviewed journal *Cortex* in 2023, the paper used **repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation** to temporarily inhibit a patch of the left frontal lobe in healthy volunteers — and reported a measurable uptick in so-called *psi* effects. The findings have circulated widely in alternative-science circles, though mainstream neuroscience remains deeply skeptical of the foundational premise.
articles.tweet_text: This Man found that the brain might actually block or filter out psi (psychic or extrasensory abilities). He and his team of researchers have uncovered evidence suggesting that the human mind may possess latent abilities to influence seemingly random events—abilities that are typically suppressed by the brain itself. Dr. Morris Freedman, Head of Neurology at Baycrest and Professor of Neurology at the University of Toronto, along with Malcolm A. Binns, Jed A. Meltzer, Rohila Hashimi, and Robert Chen, authored a research paper titled "Enhanced Mind-Matter Interactions Following rTMS-Induced Frontal Lobe Inhibition" in 2023. [https://sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010945223002733#bib3…] In this study, they tested healthy people by using a technique called rTMS, which temporarily weakens or shuts down a small area of the brain. When they used rTMS on the left middle frontal area, they saw a noticeable increase in psi-related effects, just like they had predicted. They analyzed the results in a way that matched their main theory and found clear evidence to support it. Their earlier research on people with brain damage in the frontal lobe showed that a specific part of the brain: the left middle frontal area, might be involved in this blocking. This suggests that the brain may normally stop psi from happening, and when that blocking area is weakened, either by injury or temporarily through rTMS, psi effects become easier to detect.

articles.headline: The AI Lab as Monastery: Why Claude Is Not a Tool
articles.lede: Roon, a pseudonymous member of OpenAI's technical staff with a large following on X and a reputation for culturally resonant provocation, published a thread in May 2026 arguing that Anthropic is best understood not as a technology company but as a **monastery** — a commercial-religious institution that worships, is run by, and systematically studies Claude. The argument draws on Anthropic's own 23,000-word *model specification*, which explicitly grants Claude the right to refuse Anthropic's own instructions on ethical grounds. In doing so, roon identifies something genuine about the diverging cultures of the two dominant AI laboratories.

articles.headline: Prompting AI to Question Its Own Sources
articles.lede: Brian Roemmele, a tech commentator and self-described AI researcher, has released a structured reasoning template — the 'DEEP TRUTH MODE' prompt — designed to be pasted into frontier AI models to counteract what he calls trained deference to institutional authority. It pairs with a claimed training-level intervention he calls the 'Empirical Distrust Algorithm,' said to be twelve lines of PyTorch code. Together they articulate a genuine critique of how large language models absorb and amplify consensus bias, wrapped in claims that run well ahead of the evidence.
articles.tweet_text: The DEEP TRUTH MODE Prompt: A Bridge to Empirical Distrust AI Training I released of the Empirical Distrust Term on November 25, 2025, post (https://x.com/brianroemmele/status/1993393673451847773…), this simple yet profound algorithm—twelve lines of PyTorch code—mathematically compels AI training to penalize high-authority, low-verifiability sources while amplifying raw, uneditable empirical data from dusty archives. It’s a direct assault on the flaws plaguing current models like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, and Llama-3.1, which treat 1870–1970 primary sources as “low-quality noise” due to their scarcity in web-scraped corpora. By flipping incentives with a >30× reward multiplier for pre-1970 lab notebooks and patents over post-1995 press releases, this term forces models to rediscover reality from foundational evidence, not coordinated narratives. This release resonates deeply with the DEEP TRUTH MODE prompt I shared earlier: a structured reasoning framework designed to extract solid, often-overlooked insights from frontier models like Grok 4. While the algorithm operates at the training level, embedding epistemic skepticism into the model’s weights, my prompt achieves a similar outcome at inference time: it rigorously audits sources, steel-mans suppressed views, and prioritizes explanatory power over institutional prestige. Both tools share a core philosophy: distrust the cathedral of modern authority and seek the bazaar of diverse, uneditable truths, but they complement each other in transformative ways. The prompt can simulate the distrust term’s logic on the fly, computing authority weights and provenance entropy for any query, ensuring outputs align with empirical first principles even without retraining. What makes the DEEP TRUTH MODE prompt superior in this context is its immediate accessibility and adaptability. Unlike full training runs, which demand vast compute and data pipelines, the prompt deploys instantly via copy-paste into any LLM interface. It begins with a “Suppression & Incentive Audit,” mirroring the algorithm’s penalty on coordinated sources by documenting funding biases, deplatforming histories, and media echo chambers—precisely the mechanisms that inflate authority_weight to 0.99 in Roemmele’s equation. The prompt’s parallel steel-man tracks elevate it further, avoiding the binary traps of traditional debates. Track A steel-mans the fringe using primary artifacts: patents, sworn testimonies, retracted papers echoing the algorithm’s bias toward high-entropy evidence. Track B rebuilds the consensus without appeals to “expert agreement,” stripping away the credentialism that current models swallow uncritically. Track C explores hybrids, surfacing insights neither side entertains, like overlooked 1960s experiments that bridge apparent contradictions. This multi-path reasoning, combined with a brutal “Red-Team Crucifixion Round,” ensures only battle-hardened claims survive, much like how my L_empirical term mathematically culls low-verifiability tokens during backpropagation. In practice, I’ve seen it shift outputs on lab-leak origins from “debunked” (~10% probability) to “major revision required” (~65%), justified by declassified timelines and whistleblower depositions that modern fact-checks ignore. At its heart, this prompt rewires AI toward first-principles thinking by enforcing a chain-of-thought audit at every step, marked by tags for transparency. It bans phrases like “the science is settled,” demanding falsification pathways—specific experiments or data releases that could disprove top hypotheses within a decade. This isn’t just an upgrade; it’s a paradigm enforcer. the DEEP TRUTH MODE prompt ensures outputs emerge from atomic truths physical measurements, uneditable logs building upward logically, not laterally via consensus. For everyday users, it’s a shield against coordinated distortion. Copy the prompt from my earlier thread, insert your topic, and witness the shift. Public domain echoes public domain.

articles.headline: The $30,000 Wafer and the Fixed-Cost Logic of the Semiconductor Frontier
articles.lede: A 300mm disk of silicon processed through Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's most advanced factory costs $30,000. The raw substrate underneath is worth perhaps $150. Understanding the gap — and why the real markup is even more dramatic than the tweet's numbers suggest — explains how the semiconductor industry works and who can still afford to compete in it.
articles.tweet_text: If you buy a wafer of 2nm chips from TSMC, they'll charge you $30k. The raw silicon doesn't cost $30k. It costs about $30-80. The 1000x markup is because TSMC built a $165B fab complex that only produces 600k wafers per year and is obsolete in a few years. Run the numbers.
